What you'll learn

  • Download Python 3 from python.org and install it on Windows, macOS, or a Chromebook.
  • Find and open IDLE, the editor we use in every class.
  • Run a one-line test in the IDLE Shell and recognize a working setup.
  • Fix the setup problems that catch most new students.

The first ten minutes of week 1 always split the room in two. Half the class types print("hi"), sees hi appear, and starts coding. The other half is watching a download bar crawl across the screen. This page exists so you end up in the first half.

You are installing two things, and one download gives you both. Python 3 is the interpreter: the program that reads your code and carries out each line. IDLE is the small editor that ships with Python. You will write, save, and run every program for this class in it. IDLE looks plain because it is plain. There are no plugins to set up and no settings to break, and when your code has a mistake, IDLE points straight at it.

Budget about 15 minutes, and do it before the first class.

#Three checks before you download

  • The right kind of computer. A Windows 10 or 11 PC, a Mac, or a Chromebook that allows Linux. Phones and tablets can't run IDLE.
  • Permission to install. School-managed laptops often block new software. Find out now, not five minutes before class, and tell your instructor if you're blocked.
  • The real download site. Get Python only from python.org. Lookalike "free Python download" sites sometimes bundle junk software with it.

#Install it, step by step

Pick the tab for your computer.

Windows

  1. Go to python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click the yellow Download Python button. The site detects Windows for you.
  2. Open the file you downloaded. It will be in your Downloads folder.
  3. What you see next depends on the release:
    • Recent releases set up the Python install manager. Click Install if Windows asks. A black terminal window may then ask a few yes/no questions, such as whether to add a folder to your PATH or install the latest Python now. Type y and press Enter for each one.
    • If you get the classic installer instead (a window with an Install Now button), tick Add python.exe to PATH at the bottom first, then click Install Now.
  4. Click Start and type IDLE. Open the app named something like IDLE (Python 3.15). Right-click it and choose Pin to taskbar so you can find it on class day.

If no IDLE app shows up in Start, open Terminal (or Command Prompt), type the line below, and press Enter. It starts IDLE directly.

macOS

  1. Go to python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and click Download Python. You get a .pkg installer file.
  2. Open it and click through Continue, Agree, and Install. Type your Mac password when asked.
  3. When it finishes, Finder opens a folder named Python 3.x inside Applications. IDLE lives there.
  4. Drag IDLE onto your Dock so it's one click away.

Your Mac may already have a python3 command that came with Apple's developer tools. Ignore it. Always open IDLE from Applications › Python 3.x, so you're running the same current version as the rest of the class.

Chromebook

  1. Open Settings, then go to About ChromeOS › Developers. Next to Linux development environment, click Set up and accept the defaults. Google says this can take 10 minutes or more, so start it well before class.
  2. A Terminal window opens when setup is done. Type these two commands, pressing Enter after each one. Both print lots of text while they work, which is normal.
  1. Open the app launcher and look for IDLE. Linux apps usually land together in a folder named Linux apps. If it isn't there yet, start it from the Terminal instead:

If you can't find Linux development environment in Settings at all, your school or family account has turned it off. Tell your instructor before class so we can sort out another computer.

#What success looks like

Open IDLE. The window that appears is the Shell. Its first line names your Python version, and below that sits a prompt: >>>. The prompt means "I'm listening." Click after it, type this line exactly, and press Enter:

Python answers on the very next line. Then try a little math, one line at a time. The Shell works out each answer and shows it immediately, so a full session looks like this:

That last line is 2 multiplied by itself 100 times. A calculator gives up and shows you an approximation; Python prints every digit.

If your screen matches, you're ready for class. The exact version number doesn't matter much: anything starting with 3 works, and 3.12 or newer is ideal.

📝 Note

The Shell forgets everything when you close it. That's fine for a quick test. In the next lesson you'll write programs in files that you can save and reopen.

#Fixes for the problems students actually hit

You typed the >>> yourself. The prompt is already on screen, so typing another one confuses Python. It stops with SyntaxError: invalid syntax and points at the extra arrows. Type only what comes after the prompt.

You typed Print with a capital P. Python treats capital and lowercase letters as different, so Print is a name it has never heard of. Here is the real message, including the hint newer versions add:

The last line is the one to read: print must be all lowercase.

You opened plain Python, not IDLE. On Windows there's also an app named just Python 3.x. It opens a black window with no menus. That works for one-line tests but it isn't IDLE, and it can't save files. Close it and open the app with IDLE in its name.

python is "not recognized" in a terminal on Windows. This only matters if you start IDLE from a terminal. Try py instead of python. If that fails too, run the installer again: on the classic installer choose Modify and add Python to PATH, and on the install manager answer y to the PATH question.

⚠️ Watch out

A Chromebook that says Unable to locate package after sudo apt install usually missed the first command. Run sudo apt update again, wait for it to finish, then repeat the install line.

If you're still stuck, write down the exact error message (or take a screenshot) and what you clicked just before it appeared. Send that to your instructor before the first class. "It doesn't work" takes twenty minutes to diagnose; a screenshot of the error usually takes one.

#Further reading

  • Using Python on Windows (opens in a new tab): the official guide, including the install manager and the classic installer.
  • Using Python on macOS (opens in a new tab): what the python.org installer puts on your Mac and where to find IDLE.
  • Linux on ChromeOS (opens in a new tab): Google's guide to turning on the Linux environment on a Chromebook.

What you'll learn

  • Tell IDLE's Shell window and Editor window apart, and know which one to type in.
  • Write a program in the Editor, save it as a .py file, and run it with F5.
  • Read a SyntaxError and fix the line it points at.
  • Run a setup check and share its output with your instructor.

Try this: type print("hi") in the IDLE Shell, close IDLE, and open it again. Your code is gone. The Shell is a scratchpad, perfect for testing one line and useless for anything you want to keep. Real programs live in files, and today you make your first two.

#Two windows, two jobs

IDLE has two kinds of windows. Mixing them up causes more week-1 confusion than anything else, so learn to spot them now.

Window How to recognize it What it's for
Shell Has a >>> prompt; the title starts with "IDLE Shell" Quick one-line experiments, and reading your program's output
Editor A blank page with no >>>; the title shows a file name Writing whole programs that you save and run

The rule of thumb: write in the Editor, read the results in the Shell. Every program in this course follows the same loop:

#Step 1: Open a new file

Open IDLE, which starts on the Shell. From the Shell's menu bar choose File › New File. A blank Editor window appears with untitled in its title bar, because it hasn't been saved yet.

#Step 2: Type a three-line program

Type these lines into the Editor yourself instead of pasting them. Your fingers need to learn where the quotes and parentheses go, and copying skips that practice.

Swap Ada for your own name. As you type, IDLE colors the code: text inside quotes turns green and print turns purple. Those colors are a free spell-checker. If the rest of a line suddenly turns green, you forgot a closing quote somewhere.

#Step 3: Save it as a .py file

Press Ctrl+S (Windows and Chromebook) or Cmd+S (Mac). Name the file hello.py and save it somewhere you'll find again, such as your Documents folder. The next lesson sets up a proper class folder.

The .py ending tells your computer this file is a Python program. IDLE adds it if you leave it off, but typing it yourself is a good habit.

#Step 4: Run it

Choose Run › Run Module, or press F5. (Some laptops need you to hold Fn while pressing F5.) The Shell jumps to the front, prints a divider line with the word RESTART and your file's path, and then shows your program's output, the same three lines shown under the code above.

Look closely at the last output line. You typed 12 + 30, but Python printed 42. Text inside quotes is printed exactly as written, while code outside the quotes is worked out first. Week 1 is about that difference.

💡 Tip

If IDLE asks "Source Must Be Saved. OK to Save?" when you press F5, click OK. IDLE always runs the saved copy of your file, so it wants your newest changes saved first.

#Step 5: Run the setup check

Make one more file with File › New File, type this program, save it as setup_check.py, and run it with F5.

The version line shows whichever Python is installed, so yours may differ from the one above. Anything starting with 3 is fine. Two lines here are new:

  • The first line starts with #, which makes it a comment: a note for humans that Python skips entirely.
  • import platform borrows a ready-made toolbox from Python so the program can ask which version is running. You don't need to understand imports yet.

Copy the four output lines from your Shell and paste them into the class chat at the start of the first session. That's your proof of setup.

#Step 6: Break it on purpose

Errors are normal, and professional programmers see dozens a day. The goal is to meet your first one on purpose, when you already know the cause. Open hello.py, delete the closing parenthesis at the end of the first line, save, and press F5.

IDLE refuses to run the file. It pops up a box with the error and highlights the spot in your code in red. The block above shows the same message the way Python prints it. Read it from the bottom up:

  • SyntaxError means Python couldn't understand the shape of your code, the way a sentence with no period is hard to read.
  • '(' was never closed tells you exactly what's missing.
  • line 1 and the ^ mark where the problem started.

Put the ) back, save, and run it again. You just did a complete see-it, read-it, fix-it cycle, and you'll do it hundreds of times in this course.

⚠️ Watch out

The line number in an error is where Python noticed the problem, which isn't always where you made it. A missing ) on line 1 can be reported on line 2. If the line it names looks fine, check the line above.

#Three settings worth changing now

  • Line numbers. In an Editor window choose Options › Show Line Numbers. When an error says "line 7", you'll find line 7 instantly.
  • Bigger text. Choose Options › Configure IDLE and raise the font size on the Fonts tab. (On a Mac, the settings live in the IDLE menu instead.) Your instructor will share their screen, and you'll want to see your own code just as clearly.
  • Shell history. In the Shell, press Alt+P (Ctrl+P on a Mac) to bring back the previous line you typed, so you don't have to retype it.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You type five lines into the Shell, close IDLE, and reopen it. What happened to your code?

  • The Shell never saves anything for you. Only Editor files are saved.

  • The Shell is a scratchpad. Anything you want to keep belongs in an Editor file.

  • Recent Files lists Editor files you opened or saved, not Shell sessions.

Show answer

B. The Shell is a scratchpad. Anything you want to keep belongs in an Editor file.

2You press F5 and nothing runs. Which window are you most likely in?

  • F5 runs the file in an Editor window. The Shell has no file to run.

  • That's exactly where F5 works, so the program would run.

  • Run Module is an Editor command. It needs a file.

Show answer

A. F5 runs the file in an Editor window. The Shell has no file to run.

3An error says SyntaxError on line 2, but line 2 looks perfect. Where should you look next?

  • Python reads top to bottom, so the cause is rarely below where it stopped.

  • Python often notices a missing ) or quote one line late, so check the line above.

  • A syntax error is always about the code, never about the install.

Show answer

B. Python often notices a missing ) or quote one line late, so check the line above.

#Quick checklist

  • You can open a new Editor window with File › New File.
  • You saved hello.py and setup_check.py and know which folder they're in.
  • F5 runs a file, and its output appears in the Shell.
  • You fixed a SyntaxError by reading the message.

#Further reading

  • IDLE documentation (opens in a new tab): the official guide to every IDLE menu, including Run Module, Check Module, and the Shell.
  • Automate the Boring Stuff, Chapter 1 (opens in a new tab): a free book chapter that starts with your first program and the Shell.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Know what happens in each 90-minute class and how the three lessons each week fit around it.
  • Create one course folder with a subfolder per week, and save files where you can find them.
  • Name files so they run, and avoid names that break Python's own tools.
  • Fix curly quotes, stray >>> prompts, surprise indentation, and other setup problems.

Picture week 4. Your instructor says, "Open the mission briefing you wrote in week 2." You open your Desktop and find untitled.py, untitled2.py, test.py, another test.py inside Downloads, and something called program FINAL (1).py. Class moves on while you're still clicking through them.

Ten minutes of setup now prevents that. This page covers how each class runs, where your files should live, and how to get unstuck when your computer misbehaves.

#What a week looks like

Class meets live online once a week for 1.5 hours, and each week is one module with three lessons:

  1. Notes explain the week's ideas, with short examples you can run. Skim them before class and reread them after.
  2. Code-along builds one small program step by step. In class your instructor types it and you type the same thing in your own IDLE.
  3. Practice has exercises that get harder as you go, each with a hint and a solution. Try every exercise before you open its solution.

Keep IDLE open for the whole class. Watching someone else type code feels like learning, but your hands only learn it when you type it yourself, mistakes included.

💡 Tip

When you're stuck, paste your code and the complete error message into the chat. "It doesn't work" is almost impossible to help with. "Line 3 says NameError: name 'nmae' is not defined" usually gets fixed in seconds.

#One folder for the whole course

Create a folder named C4T-Python with one folder inside it for each week:

Put it somewhere simple, like Documents on Windows or a Mac. On a Chromebook, make it inside Linux files in the Files app. The Linux copy of IDLE can't see your Downloads or Google Drive folders unless you share them with Linux, so files saved there seem to vanish.

Move hello.py and setup_check.py from the last lesson into setup/. Then open one of them in IDLE with File › Open from its new home, so File › Recent Files points to the right place.

#File names that work

Good file names are short, lowercase, and say what the program does, with underscores instead of spaces:

  • Good: week2_mission_briefing.py, ex3_temperature.py, rocket_launch.py
  • Bad: untitled.py, My Program FINAL (2).py, test.py

Two naming rules matter more than the rest.

Always end with .py. A file saved as hello.txt or hello.py.txt won't get IDLE's colors, and F5 won't run it.

Never name a file after one of Python's own tools. Python checks your folder before its own library, so a file of yours called random.py hides the real random tool. In week 3 you'll write a game that starts with import random. If a homemade random.py sits in the same folder, Python 3.13 and newer end the error with this line (your own folder path appears in the middle):

Older versions stop after no attribute 'choice', which is baffling if you don't know the cause. Avoid random.py, math.py, turtle.py, string.py, and time.py.

Test the new folder with a tiny program. Save it as week1/where_am_i.py and run it with F5:

#Fixes for the problems students hit most

#F5 does nothing

You're probably in the Shell, not the Editor. F5 only runs a file that's open in an Editor window. Use File › New File or File › Open first.

#Python says "invalid character" about your quotes

Code copied from a word processor, a chat app, or a slide deck often has curly quotes “ ” in place of straight ones ". They look almost the same to you, but Python only accepts the straight kind:

The U+201C in the message is the code number for a left curly quote. Delete both quote marks and retype them in IDLE, which always types straight quotes.

#You pasted from the Shell and got "invalid syntax"

Copying lines out of the Shell often brings the >>> prompt along. In a file, the prompt is just junk characters:

Delete every >>> and keep only the code after it.

#Python says "unexpected indent"

Spaces at the start of a line mean something in Python, so a stray space or two breaks the program:

Move the second print back to the left edge. In week 3 you'll start indenting lines on purpose, and then the spaces will matter in the other direction.

#Windows: python is not recognized in a terminal

IDLE doesn't need the terminal, so you can ignore this during class. If you want it fixed, try py in place of python. If that fails too, run the Python installer again and make sure Python is added to PATH.

#Mac: python says "command not found"

On a Mac the terminal command is python3, not python. IDLE isn't affected.

#Chromebook: IDLE won't open, or your files are missing

Check that Linux finished setting up, then type python3 -m idlelib in the Terminal. If files seem to have disappeared, open the Files app and look in Linux files.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Which of these file names is safest for this week's exercise?

  • That hides Python's own random tool, which you'll need for games in week 3.

  • It works, but spaces and capitals make it harder to find and type. Use underscores.

  • Short, lowercase, underscores, ends in .py, and says what it is.

  • A .txt file won't run with F5 or get IDLE's colors.

Show answer

C. Short, lowercase, underscores, ends in .py, and says what it is.

2You paste code from a slide and get SyntaxError: invalid character '“' (U+201C). What's the fix?

  • Nothing is wrong with Python. The code has a character it doesn't accept.

  • Curly quotes came along with the paste. IDLE types straight quotes, which Python accepts.

  • Extra leading spaces cause a different error, unexpected indent.

Show answer

B. Curly quotes came along with the paste. IDLE types straight quotes, which Python accepts.

#Further reading

  • Using Python on Unix platforms (opens in a new tab): official notes that apply to the Linux setup on Chromebooks.
  • Python on Windows FAQ (opens in a new tab): answers to the most common "how do I run a .py file" questions on Windows.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Predict the order a program's output appears in, because Python runs lines top to bottom.
  • Use print() to show text, numbers, and calculations, and know when quotes matter.
  • Shape output with commas, sep, end, \n, and string repetition.
  • Write comments that explain your code, and use # to switch a line off.
  • Read the two errors beginners hit most with print().

Here are two lines of Python that differ by exactly two characters:

The first prints 2 + 3. The second prints 5. Those two quote marks are the difference between "show this text" and "work this out", and most of this week comes down to knowing which one you mean.

#Python follows your lines in order, every time

A program is a list of instructions in a text file. When you press F5, Python starts at line 1, does exactly what it says, moves to line 2, and keeps going to the bottom. It never skips ahead, never guesses what you meant, and never rearranges anything.

Step through this one and watch the output panel fill in, one line per step:

Swap the first two lines in your own copy and the first two lines of output swap with them. The order you write is the order you get.

#The parts of a print() call

Every piece has a job:

  • print is the name of a function, a built-in command that does one job. This one displays things in the Shell.
  • The parentheses ( ) hold whatever you want displayed. No parentheses, no printing.
  • The quotes mark where a piece of text starts and stops. Programmers call a piece of text a string, as in a string of characters.

Double quotes "like this" and single quotes 'like this' both work. Close a string with the same kind of quote you opened it with.

#Quotes mean "show this exactly"

Inside quotes, Python treats every character as plain text and copies it to the screen. Outside quotes, Python treats what you wrote as something to calculate first, then prints the answer.

Look at the last two lines. When you give print() several items separated by commas, it prints them all on one line with one space between each. That's why "I have", 3 comes out as I have 3 even though you never typed that space. In the last line, 3 + 2 sits outside the quotes, so Python adds it up before printing.

#Shaping the output: sep, end, and friends

print() takes a few extra settings for laying out text exactly how you want. Predict each line of output before you look at the result.

What each trick does:

  • sep="-" replaces the space between items with whatever you choose. Here the three pieces of the date are glued with dashes.
  • end="" stops print() from starting a new line afterward, so the next print() keeps writing on the same line. Three calls built Loading... done!.
  • print() with nothing inside prints an empty line, which is handy for spacing.
  • \n inside a string means "start a new line here". You type two characters, a backslash and an n, but Python treats them as one.
  • Mixing quotes lets one kind sit inside the other. Use double quotes on the outside when the text has an apostrophe, like "It's".
  • "=" * 20 repeats a string 20 times. It's the quickest way to draw a divider.

The end="" idea is the one that trips people up, because the effect shows up on the next line of code. Step through it and watch where each piece lands:

#Comments: notes for humans

A comment starts with #. Python ignores everything from the # to the end of that line, so comments are free to say anything. Use them to explain why code exists, to label sections, and to switch a line off without deleting it.

The pickle step never prints, because its line starts with #. Turning code into a comment like this is called commenting out. It's the fastest way to test "what happens without this line?" without losing the line. In IDLE you can select several lines and choose Format › Comment Out Region to do them all at once, and Format › Uncomment Region to bring them back.

📝 Note

A # inside quotes is just a character, not a comment. print("Use a #2 pencil") prints the whole sentence, #2 included.

#Habits that make code readable

Code gets read far more often than it gets written: by classmates, by your instructor, and by you next week when you've forgotten how it works. A few habits help a lot:

  • Start each file with a comment that says what the program does.
  • Use blank lines to separate sections, like paragraphs in an essay.
  • Comment the why, not the obvious. # print hello above print("hello") adds nothing. # Banner shown before the game starts tells the reader something the code can't.
  • Put one space after #, and two spaces before a comment that sits at the end of a line of code. That's what Python's official style guide, PEP 8, recommends.

#The two errors you'll meet first

Forgetting the quotes. Without quotes, Python thinks Hello is the name of something it should already know about. It doesn't, so it stops:

NameError means "I don't recognize that name." The fix is print("Hello").

Forgetting the closing quote. Now the string never ends, and Python reaches the end of the line still inside it:

"Unterminated string literal" is Python's way of saying "this text never stops." Add the missing " before the ).

⚠️ Watch out

Three more slips to watch for: Print with a capital P (Python is case-sensitive, so it's a different name), a missing ) at the end of a line, and curly quotes “ ” pasted from a document. When you see any error, read the last line first. It names the kind of error and usually says what's wrong.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does print("5", 5 + 5) show?

  • Only the first 5 is in quotes. The 5 + 5 is outside them, so Python adds it first.

  • The string "5" prints as-is, the sum becomes 10, and the comma adds one space between them.

  • Commas in print() always put a space between items unless you change sep.

Show answer

B. The string "5" prints as-is, the sum becomes 10, and the comma adds one space between them.

2A program runs print("A", "B", "C", sep=""), then print("D", end="!"), then print("E"). What appears?

  • sep="" removes the spaces, and end="!" stops the line break after D.

  • No separator joins A, B, and C. Then end="!" replaces the line break, so E lands right after the !.

  • The first print() still ends with a normal line break. Only the second one changed its end.

Show answer

B. No separator joins A, B, and C. Then end="!" replaces the line break, so E lands right after the !.

3Which line prints nothing at all?

  • The # is inside quotes, so it's just text, and the whole string prints.

  • This prints an empty line. You'd see the gap.

  • The line starts with #, so Python skips all of it.

Show answer

C. The line starts with #, so Python skips all of it.

4You run print("Score:" 10) and get a SyntaxError. What's missing?

  • Numbers don't need quotes. print("Score:", 10) works fine.

  • Each item you give print() must be separated by a comma.

  • One pair holds everything you want to print.

Show answer

B. Each item you give print() must be separated by a comma.

Key takeaways

  • Python runs a program from the first line to the last, in order.
  • Text in quotes prints exactly as typed; code outside quotes is worked out first.
  • Commas in print() add a space between items. sep changes that space, and end changes the line break at the end.
  • \n starts a new line inside a string, and "=" * 20 repeats a string.
  • # starts a comment. Use comments to explain why, and to switch lines off while testing.
  • Read error messages from the bottom line up.

#Further reading

  • The print() function (opens in a new tab): the official reference, including sep and end.
  • PEP 8: Comments (opens in a new tab): the official style guide's advice on writing comments that help.

What you'll learn

  • Plan a program with comments before writing any code.
  • Draw borders and ASCII art with string repetition and escaped backslashes.
  • Combine sep and end to put exactly the right characters on each line.
  • Find and fix an output bug by comparing what you got with what you wanted.

The Riverside Animal Shelter is holding an adoption day on Saturday, and they want a poster. They don't have a designer. They have you, and you have print(). By the end of class you'll have a program of about 30 lines that prints this:

Every line of it comes from a single print() call, or two calls working together. In IDLE, choose File › New File and save the empty file as week1/adoption_poster.py before you write anything.

#Step 1: Write the plan as comments

Experienced programmers often write the outline before the code. Type these comments first. They do nothing when you run them, but they give the file a shape to fill in, and later they'll tell a reader where each part of the poster lives.

Press F5. The Shell restarts and then shows nothing at all. That's correct: a file of only comments is a program with no instructions.

#Step 2: The border and the title

Under the "Top border and title" comment, add three lines:

"*" * 32 repeats the star 32 times, so you don't have to type or count them. The middle line is also exactly 32 characters wide, which is why the box lines up. If your right edge looks crooked, count the spaces on each side of the title.

#Step 3: Draw the cat, and meet the backslash

Under "Picture", the obvious first try is to type the cat's ears just as they look:

The error says the string never ended, and Python even guesses why: perhaps you escaped the end quote? Inside a string, a backslash \ doesn't mean "backslash". It means "the next character is special". You already met \n, which means "new line". Here, the last \ grabbed the closing quote and turned it into an ordinary character, so the string has no end.

To print one real backslash, type two of them: \\. Python reads the pair as a single backslash character.

In your file, add a print() before and after the cat to give it some breathing room.

#Step 4: About the pet

Now the details. Commas let you mix text and numbers on one line:

Compare the last line with the target poster. There's a stray bar right after Likes:. That's because sep goes between every pair of items, and the label counts as an item. We want bars between the three likes, but a plain space after the label.

The fix: print the label by itself with end=" ", so the next print() continues on the same line, and give only the likes the " | " separator.

Step through the fixed version and watch the cursor stay on the same line after the first call:

Bugs like this are a normal part of building anything. You ran the code, compared the output with what you wanted, spotted the difference, and changed one thing. That's most of programming.

#Step 5: Event details

The date line combines both settings: sep glues the parts of the date with dashes, and end="" keeps the cursor on the same line so the time lands right after it.

Notice the space at the start of " @ 10am". Because the first call ended with nothing at all, that space is the only thing separating 21 from @.

#Step 6: The finished program

Add a bottom border under the last comment, and your file should look like this:

Run it with F5 and check it against the poster at the top of the page. Then read the file from top to bottom. Thanks to the section comments, anyone could find the part that prints the date in a couple of seconds without running anything. The comment above the cat explains the one line that would otherwise look like a typo.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the finished program print the label Likes: with its own print() call?

  • print() accepts as many items as you like.

  • sep goes between every item in one call. Splitting the label off keeps the bar out of it.

  • They work fine together, as the date line in Step 5 shows.

Show answer

B. sep goes between every item in one call. Splitting the label off keeps the bar out of it.

2What would print("C:\\Users") show?

  • The pair of backslashes is one escape code, so only one backslash prints.

  • \\ stands for a single backslash character.

  • The string is properly closed; the doubled backslash doesn't touch the quote.

Show answer

B. \\ stands for a single backslash character.

3What does the date line print if you delete end="" from the first call?

  • Without end="", the first print() finishes with a normal line break.

  • The default end is a new line, so the second call starts a fresh line.

  • sep=" - " is still there, so the dashes stay.

Show answer

B. The default end is a new line, so the second call starts a fresh line.

Key takeaways

  • Writing the plan as comments first gives your program a shape and labels for later.
  • String repetition like "*" * 32 draws borders without counting characters.
  • A backslash starts an escape code inside a string. Use \\ to print one real backslash.
  • sep goes between every item in a single print(), so split a call when only some items should be separated.
  • end="" lets two print() calls build one line of output.

What you'll learn

  • Create and update variables, and read = as "gets".
  • Tell the four basic types apart: str, int, float, and bool.
  • Drop variables into text with f-strings.
  • Ask the user a question with input(), and convert the answer with int() or float() before doing math.

Here's a tiny calculator. It asks for two numbers and adds them. Type 7 and 3, and it reports the sum:

Seventy-three. Python didn't crash and didn't warn you; it just quietly did the wrong thing. By the end of this page you'll know exactly why, and the fix is a single word.

Last week every program printed the same thing every time it ran. A game needs to remember your score, though, and a quiz needs to know your answer. So this week your programs learn to store values and to ask for them.

#A variable is a name stuck on a value

Think of a variable as a sticky label. You write a name on it and press it onto a value. Later you say the name and Python hands back whatever the label is stuck to. You create one with a single equals sign:

Read = as "gets", not "equals". score = 10 means "score gets 10". That's why score = score + 5 makes sense in Python even though it's nonsense in math class. Python always works out the right side first, using the current value of score, and only then moves the label to the result. This is called assignment.

Step through it and watch the score label move from 0 to 10 to 15 in the variables panel:

Notice that print(player) has no quotes. Without quotes, Python looks the name up and prints its value. With quotes, print("player") prints the word player.

#Rules for names

  • Letters, digits, and underscores only, and a name can't start with a digit. level2 works; 2level is a SyntaxError.
  • No spaces. Use underscores: high_score, not high score.
  • Capitals count. Score and score are two different variables.
  • Choose names that say what the value means. lives beats x, and ticket_price beats p.

#Every value has a type

A value's type decides what you can do with it. You can add two numbers, but you can't sensibly multiply a name by a name. Ask Python for any value's type with type():

Type Short for Examples Use it for
str string "Maya", "42", "" Text of any kind
int integer 3, -10, 0 Whole numbers: counts, scores
float floating-point number 2.5, -0.75, 3.0 Numbers with a decimal point
bool Boolean True, False Yes/no facts

The details that trip people up:

  • "42" in quotes is a string: the character 4 followed by the character 2. It isn't a number until you convert it.
  • 3.0 is a float, because of the decimal point, even though it's a whole number.
  • True and False start with a capital letter and have no quotes. Next week your programs will make decisions with them.
  • Floats are stored in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 prints 0.30000000000000004. Every programming language does this, and it isn't a bug in your code.

#f-strings: drop variables straight into text

Put an f right before the opening quote and you get an f-string. Anything inside curly braces { } gets worked out and placed into the text:

With commas, print() decides where the spaces go. With an f-string, you decide, so punctuation like the period after 13 sits exactly where you put it.

#input(): ask the person at the keyboard

input() shows a message, waits for the user to type something and press Enter, and hands back what they typed. Store that answer in a variable:

End your prompt with a space, like "What is your name? ". Otherwise the user's answer is jammed against the question mark.

#Why input() always hands you text

Here's the rule behind the 73: input() always gives back a string, even when the user types digits. Watch what happens when you try to do math with the answer:

type(age) says str. Then Python refuses to add the number 1 to the text "13", because "add a number to some text" has no sensible meaning.

Back to the calculator. first held "7" and second held "3", both strings. For strings, + doesn't add, it joins: "7" + "3" is "73". No error, because joining two strings is perfectly legal. That's what makes the bug sneaky.

#Converting between types

Every basic type has a function with the same name that converts a value into that type:

  • int() turns a string like "42" into a whole number. Given a float, it chops off the decimal part instead of rounding, so int(9.99) is 9.
  • float() turns a string like "3.5" into a decimal number.
  • str() turns a number into text, so you can join it to other text with +.
  • + means different things for different types: it adds numbers and joins strings.

The usual pattern wraps input() inside the conversion, so the variable holds a number from the start. Here's the calculator, fixed:

That's the one-word fix, applied twice. Use float() instead when the answer might have a decimal point, like a height in meters or a price.

#What usually goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

Converting something that isn't a number. If the user types twelve, int() gives up with ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve'. Typing 3.5 into int() causes the same error, since int() only reads whole numbers. Use float() when decimals are allowed.

  • Joining a number to a string with +. "Your score is " + 95 raises a TypeError. Use an f-string, a comma in print(), or str(95).
  • Using a variable before creating it. Python runs top to bottom, so print(total) above total = 10 raises NameError: name 'total' is not defined.
  • Typos in names. scroe isn't score. IDLE won't catch it until the line runs.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What does this print: x = 5, then x = x * 2, then x = x - 3, then print(x)?

  • Each assignment replaces the old value, so x doesn't stay at 5.

  • 5 becomes 10, then 10 becomes 7. The right side is always worked out first using the current value.

  • No quotes around x, so Python prints its value, not the letter.

Show answer

B. 5 becomes 10, then 10 becomes 7. The right side is always worked out first using the current value.

2A program runs n = input("Pick a number: ") and the user types 4. What does print(n * 3) show?

  • That would happen if n were the number 4. input() gave back the string "4".

  • A string times 3 repeats the string, just like "=" * 20.

  • Multiplying a string by a whole number is allowed. It's adding a number to a string that fails.

Show answer

B. A string times 3 repeats the string, just like "=" * 20.

3Which line crashes?

  • The string holds only digits, so it converts to 42.

  • int() can't read a decimal point from a string. Use float("3.5").

  • float() happily reads whole numbers too, giving 3.0.

  • Any number can become a string.

Show answer

B. int() can't read a decimal point from a string. Use float("3.5").

4You're asking "How tall are you in meters?" How should you read the answer?

  • This leaves the answer as text, so any math with it will fail or misbehave.

  • 1.6 would crash int(), and heights usually have decimals.

  • A float can hold 1.6, and it works for whole numbers like 2 too.

Show answer

C. A float can hold 1.6, and it works for whole numbers like 2 too.

Key takeaways

  • A variable is a name for a value. = means "gets", and the right side is worked out first.
  • The four basic types are str (text), int (whole numbers), float (decimals), and bool (True/False).
  • f-strings like f"{name} is {age}" put values into text exactly where you want them.
  • input() always returns a string. Wrap it in int() or float() before doing math.
  • + adds numbers but joins strings, which is how 7 + 3 becomes 73.

  • Built-in types (opens in a new tab): the official reference for int, float, str, and bool.
  • Formatted string literals (opens in a new tab): the official tutorial's section on f-strings.
  • Automate the Boring Stuff, Chapter 1 (opens in a new tab): variables, data types, input(), and conversions, with plenty of examples.

What you'll learn

  • Store fixed facts in variables at the top of a program so they're easy to change.
  • Choose the right conversion for each input(): none, int(), or float().
  • Spot a quiet type bug that gives a wrong answer without any error.
  • Lay out a neat report with f-strings and round long decimals with round().

Mission control needs a program that interviews the commander before launch and prints a briefing card. It has to remember four answers, turn some of them into numbers, do some fuel math, and print everything in tidy columns. That's every idea from this week's Notes in one program.

Here's how the data flows through it. Text comes in from the keyboard, some of it gets converted, the numbers get crunched, and everything lands on the card:

In IDLE, create week2/mission_briefing.py and follow along.

#Step 1: Store the facts that never change

Some values are known before the program even starts. Store them in variables at the top, where they're easy to find and change later.

That's three of the four basic types already: ship_name is a str, fuel_per_day is a float because of its decimal point, and supplies_ready is a bool. The print() at the bottom is only there to check your work. Delete it once you've seen the output.

#Step 2: Ask questions, and catch a sneaky bug

Next, ask for the commander's name, the destination, and the crew size. Each crew member eats three meals a day, so multiply to get meals per day. Run it and answer Rivera, Mars, and 4:

Four hundred forty-four meals a day. There's no error message, but the answer is badly wrong. Step through the important part and watch the variables panel. Look at what crew actually holds: the quote marks around it give it away.

input() returned the string "4", and a string times 3 repeats the string, exactly like "=" * 32 repeats an equals sign. Quiet bugs like this are the dangerous ones, because nothing warns you. You only catch them by checking whether the answer makes sense.

Fix it by converting the answer to an int:

Now crew * 3 gives 12. Leave commander and planet alone: they really are text, and converting them would make no sense.

#Step 3: Fuel math with floats

Fuel can be a fraction, like 37.5 tons, so convert it with float(), not int(). Then divide by the fuel burned per day to see how many days it lasts. Try it with 50:

Division with / always gives a float, and 50 divided by 3 goes on forever, so Python shows every digit it stores. round(value, 1) rounds to one decimal place, which a commander can actually read at a glance.

💡 Tip

For every input(), ask one question: "Will I do math with this?" If yes, wrap it in int() for whole numbers or float() for numbers that might have decimals. If no, leave it as a string.

#Step 4: Print the briefing card

Now put it together. The f-strings use spaces after each label so the values line up in a neat column. Here's the complete program, run with Rivera, Mars, 4, and 50:

Two lines of the card are worth a closer look. The commander typed 50, but the card says Fuel loaded: 50.0 tons, because float() always produces a number with a decimal point. And Supplies ready: True shows that a Boolean prints as the word True.

The program is organized the way most programs are: fixed facts, then input, then calculations, then output. When something goes wrong, that order tells you which section to look in.

#Step 5: Try to break it

Testing means typing what a real user might type, not just the answers you hoped for. Run it again and answer four for the crew size:

int() only understands digits, so the word four stops the program with a ValueError. For now, the defense is a prompt that makes it obvious what to type. In a few weeks you'll learn how to check an answer and ask again.

Then try a few more, and predict each result before you press Enter:

  • A crew of 0. What happens to meals per day?
  • Fuel of 37.5. Does it still work? (It should, because fuel uses float().)
  • A crew of 2.5. Why does this crash, and is crashing actually reasonable for half a person?

⚠️ Watch out

If you rename a variable, rename it everywhere. Changing crew to crew_size on the input line but not in the f-strings gives NameError: name 'crew' is not defined, pointing at the first line that still uses the old name.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why is crew converted with int() but fuel with float()?

  • Speed isn't the reason. The choice depends on what values make sense.

  • int() would crash on 37.5, and a crew of 2.5 people should be rejected.

  • Any input() can be converted with either function.

Show answer

B. int() would crash on 37.5, and a crew of 2.5 people should be rejected.

2Before the fix, why did 4 crew members give 444 meals with no error?

  • No arithmetic happened at all.

  • Repeating a string is legal, so Python had nothing to complain about.

  • The result was a string, "444", not a number of any kind.

Show answer

B. Repeating a string is legal, so Python had nothing to complain about.

3Why store fuel_per_day = 3.0 in a variable instead of typing 3.0 in the division?

  • The name also tells a reader what the 3.0 means, which a bare number doesn't.

  • fuel / 3.0 works fine. The variable is for people, not for Python.

  • The result is identical either way.

Show answer

A. The name also tells a reader what the 3.0 means, which a bare number doesn't.

Key takeaways

  • Put fixed facts in clearly named variables at the top of the program.
  • Convert each input() based on how you'll use it: int() for counts, float() for measurements, nothing for text.
  • A string times a number repeats the string, so a missing conversion can give a wrong answer without any error.
  • / always gives a float. round(value, 1) makes long decimals readable.
  • Test with answers a real user might give, including ones you expect to fail.

#Make it yours

  • Ask for the mission length in days, then print how many meals the whole trip needs: crew * 3 * mission_days.
  • Store fuel_needed = mission_days * fuel_per_day and print it beside the fuel loaded, so the commander can compare the two.
  • Change ship_name to your own ship. Because it's a variable, you change it in one place and the card updates everywhere.

  • Built-in functions (opens in a new tab): the official reference for input(), int(), float(), and round().
  • Numeric types (opens in a new tab): how Python's numbers behave, including what / does.

Need a hint?

input() returned the string "20", and a string times 7 repeats it seven times. Converting with int() fixes the math, but then the program crashes on the last line:

Now pages_per_week is the number 140, and + can't join a string to a number. An f-string fixes that too, because it converts whatever is in the braces to text for you:

#Exercise 6: Swap two variables

Start with these two lines:

Add lines that swap the values, so that the program then prints left is dog, right is cat. The rule: you may not type "cat" or "dog" again.

Need a hint?

Try left = right followed by right = left and trace it in your table. What happened to "cat"? You need somewhere to keep it safe for a moment, the way you'd use a third cup to swap the drinks in two full cups.

The obvious attempt, left = right then right = left, leaves both variables holding "dog", because the first line throws away "cat" before anything saved it. A third variable holds it for one step. Python also has a shortcut, left, right = right, left, which you'll see in other people's code.

#Challenge: Bill splitter

Target runs:

Need a hint?

Decide on a type for each of the three answers first. Then remember that 15 percent means 15 divided by 100. Work out the tip, then the total, then each share, storing each in its own variable.

Show solution

Each answer gets the type that fits it. The bill can have cents, so it's a float. The tip percent and the number of people are whole numbers, so they're ints. Dividing by 100 turns 18 into 0.18. What you'll learn

  • Use //, %, and **, and predict results using the order of operations.
  • Write comparisons that answer True or False.
  • Make a program choose one path with if, elif, and else, and order the conditions correctly.
  • Combine conditions with and, or, and not.
  • Fix the classic condition bugs: = for ==, missing colons, and or written like English.

Here's a grader with a bug in it:

A 95 should earn the A message, but it never appears, for 95 or 100 or any score at all. There's no error and no warning. By the end of this page you'll see exactly why, and the fix is swapping two lines.

Every program you've written so far ran every line, every time. Real programs choose. A thermostat turns on the heat only when it's cold. A game says "Game over" only when your lives hit zero. This week your programs learn to ask a yes/no question and pick a path.

#Three operators you haven't used yet

You know +, -, *, and /. Python has three more that turn out to be surprisingly handy:

Operator Name 7 ? 2 gives Think of it as
/ divide 3.5 The exact answer, always a float
// floor divide 3 How many whole groups?
% modulo (remainder) 1 How many are left over?
** power 49 7 × 7

// and % are a team. Share 135 minutes into hours, and // tells you how many whole hours fit while % tells you the minutes left over:

% is also the standard test for even numbers. n % 2 is 0 when n is even and 1 when it's odd. You'll use that in the practice set.

#Which operator goes first

Python follows the order from math class: parentheses first, then **, then *, /, //, and %, and finally + and -. Operators at the same level go left to right.

When you're not sure, add parentheses. They cost nothing and make your intent obvious to the next reader.

#Comparisons ask a yes/no question

A comparison checks something and answers with a Boolean, True or False:

The six comparisons are == (equal), != (not equal), <, >, <=, and >=. Watch the double equals sign. A single = stores a value; == asks whether two values match. String comparisons are exact, so "cat" == "Cat" is False because of one capital letter.

#if: run some lines only when a condition is true

An if statement runs the lines under it only when its condition is True:

Two details make it work. The if line ends with a colon. The lines that belong to it are indented by four spaces, and IDLE does that for you after you type the colon and press Enter. The last print() isn't indented, so it isn't part of the if: it runs no matter what. Change lives to 3 and run it again; only the last line prints.

#if, elif, else: pick exactly one path

Often there are more than two possibilities. elif (short for "else if") adds another condition to check, and else catches everything left over. Python checks the conditions from the top down and runs the block under the first one that's True. Then it skips the rest of the chain.

Here's that chart as code. Step through it with an answer of 72 and watch which lines get skipped:

72 fails the first check, passes the second, and Python jumps straight past everything else in the chain to the last line. It never even looks at >= 32, even though 72 is bigger than 32. The same program with 40 lands one branch lower:

You can have as many elif branches as you need. else has no condition and is optional; without it, a chain can end up running nothing.

#Why the grader never says "Amazing"

Now the bug from the top makes sense. With a score of 95, Python checks score >= 70 first. That's True, so it prints "You passed." and skips the rest of the chain. The elif score >= 90 never gets a turn, for any score.

The fix is to put the strictest condition first:

When conditions overlap, order them from the narrowest to the broadest.

#Combine conditions with and, or, not

  • and is True only when both sides are True.
  • or is True when at least one side is True.
  • not flips a Boolean: not True is False.
a b a and b a or b
True True True True
True False False True
False True False True
False False False False

Here they are making real decisions at a movie theater:

The third if prints nothing: has_ticket is True, so not has_ticket is False. When you mix them, Python applies not first, then and, then or. Add parentheses to make longer conditions clear.

#The bugs everyone writes once

Comparing input without converting it. input() gives a string, and Python won't compare text to a number:

Fix: age = int(input("How old are you? ")).

Using = where you meant ==. Python catches this one and even suggests the fix:

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting the colon gives SyntaxError: expected ':'. Forgetting to indent the line after an if gives IndentationError: expected an indented block after 'if' statement. Both stop the program before it runs a single line, and IDLE highlights where.

Writing or like English. This reads fine out loud, and it's wrong:

The color is blue, yet it says "Warm color". Python reads the condition as (color == "red") or ("orange"), and a non-empty string like "orange" counts as true all by itself. Repeat the comparison on both sides of or:

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What is 17 % 5?

  • That's 17 // 5, the number of whole fives in 17.

  • Three fives make 15, and 2 is left over. % gives the remainder.

  • That's 17 / 5, the exact division.

Show answer

B. Three fives make 15, and 2 is left over. % gives the remainder.

2With x = 50, what does this chain print? if x > 10: prints "big", elif x > 40: prints "huge", else: prints "small".

  • x > 10 is True, so Python runs that branch and skips the rest of the chain.

  • Only one branch in a chain ever runs, even if several conditions are true.

  • The conditions are checked top to bottom, and x > 10 comes first.

Show answer

A. x > 10 is True, so Python runs that branch and skips the rest of the chain.

3age = 15 and has_pass = False. Which condition is True?

  • and needs both sides, and has_pass is False.

  • or needs only one side, and age >= 13 is True.

  • age >= 13 is True, and not flips it to False.

Show answer

B. or needs only one side, and age >= 13 is True.

4Why does if color == "red" or "orange": say "Warm color" for blue?

  • It doesn't ignore it. It evaluates "orange" on its own.

  • Each side of or is its own condition. Write color == "orange" on the right.

  • They don't, and capitals aren't involved here anyway.

Show answer

B. Each side of or is its own condition. Write color == "orange" on the right.

Key takeaways

  • // gives whole groups, % gives the remainder, and ** raises to a power.
  • Comparisons like == and >= produce True or False. One = stores; two == compare.
  • An if line ends with a colon, and its block is indented four spaces.
  • In an if/elif/else chain, only the first true branch runs, so put the strictest condition first.
  • and needs both sides true, or needs one, and not flips. Repeat the full comparison on each side of or.

What you'll learn

  • Turn a list of real-world rules into if, elif, and else statements.
  • Test every branch, especially the boundary values where the answer flips.
  • Store a yes/no answer as a Boolean and use it in later conditions.
  • Use // for a "one free in every three" deal, and parentheses to group and with or.

The Thunderbolt is the tallest coaster in the park, and its ticket booth runs on Python. The park's rules:

  • Riders must be at least 48 inches tall.
  • Kids 12 and under pay $8 a ride, seniors 65 and up pay $10, and everyone else pays $15.
  • Season pass holders ride free.
  • Every third ride is on the house.
  • Season pass holders and seniors get the Fast Lane, but only if they're tall enough to ride at all.

Each rule is one small decision. Here's the whole booth as a picture before we write any of it:

You'll add one rule at a time. Save your work as week3/coaster_booth.py.

#Step 1: The height check

Start with the rule that matters most: too short means no ride.

That's one side of the line. Now test the other side with a shorter rider:

The f-string does subtraction right inside the braces, so Mia learns exactly how far she has to go. Storing 48 in min_height means that if the park changes the rule, you edit one line, and the message updates too.

#Step 2: Price by age

Three prices means three outcomes, which calls for if, elif, and else. Try this in a scratch file first:

Now test the boundaries, the ages where the price changes. Predict each one before you run it:

Age typed Price you should see Why
12 $8 12 <= 12 is True
13 $15 Too old for the kid price, too young for the senior price
64 $15 One year short of the senior price
65 $10 65 >= 65 is True

Step through the senior case and watch Python skip the kid branch:

Bugs love boundaries. If you'd typed age < 12 instead of age <= 12, a 12-year-old would pay the adult price. A 10-year-old and a 30-year-old would still get the right answer, so only a test at the boundary catches it.

#Step 3: Season passes as a Boolean

Ask whether the rider has a season pass. People type the answer every way imaginable: yes, Yes, YES. Adding .lower() to a string gives you an all-lowercase copy, so you only have to compare against one spelling:

The comparison answer.lower() == "yes" produces True or False, and we store that Boolean in has_pass. Later code can then say if has_pass:, which reads almost like English. Try no and Yes too.

#Step 4: Every third ride is free

The deal is one free ride in every three. Floor division answers exactly that question: how many complete groups of three are in the number of rides?

Seven rides hold two complete groups of three, so 7 // 3 is 2, and the rider pays for 5 rides at $15. The parentheses in (rides - free_rides) * price make the subtraction happen before the multiplication. Without them, Python would multiply first and charge something very strange.

#Step 5: The Fast Lane

Pass holders and seniors skip the line, but only if they can ride. In words: tall enough, and (has a pass or is a senior). Here it is, tested on a 70-year-old who is only 44 inches tall:

Correct: she can't ride, so no Fast Lane. Now delete the parentheses and run the same rider again:

Python does and before or, so without parentheses it reads the condition as (height >= min_height and has_pass) or age >= 65. Being 70 is enough to make that True, and the booth hands a Fast Lane pass to someone who isn't allowed on the ride.

#Step 6: The complete booth

Here's everything together, organized into sections. This run is Jay: 60 inches, 16 years old, with a season pass, buying 5 rides.

Notice that the age chain always runs and sets a price, and then the season pass check can overwrite it with 0. Order is doing real work here: if the pass check came first, the age chain would overwrite the free price.

Now run your own copy for three more riders. Predict each result first, then check:

Rider Height Age Pass Rides What should happen
Leo 52 13 no 7 Welcome, 2 free rides, $75, no Fast Lane
Grandma Rose 62 70 no 2 Welcome, $20, Fast Lane
Mia 44 9 Yes 4 Sorry, 4 more inches, no Fast Lane

Mia has a season pass but still gets no Fast Lane, because the and insists she's tall enough first. That one line encodes a rule that's easy to get wrong.

⚠️ Watch out

Check your indentation carefully. The three print() lines under else: must all be indented by the same four spaces. If one isn't, you'll get an IndentationError, or worse, a line that runs for the wrong riders.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the pass check (if has_pass: price = 0) come after the age chain?

  • The age chain always sets a price. Putting the pass check last lets it have the final word.

  • Python lets you put conditions in any order. The order here is about getting the right answer.

  • Swap them and every pass holder pays full price again.

Show answer

A. The age chain always sets a price. Putting the pass check last lets it have the final word.

2Which test would catch someone typing age < 12 instead of age <= 12?

  • 10 is under 12 either way, so both versions say $8.

  • 12 <= 12 is true but 12 < 12 is false, so only this boundary shows the difference.

  • Both versions charge a 30-year-old $15.

Show answer

B. 12 <= 12 is true but 12 < 12 is false, so only this boundary shows the difference.

3A rider buys 8 rides. How many are free?

  • Three free rides would need 9 rides.

  • 8 // 3 is 2: two complete groups of three, with 2 rides left over.

  • // drops the remainder and gives a whole number.

Show answer

B. 8 // 3 is 2: two complete groups of three, with 2 rides left over.

Key takeaways

  • Turn each rule into one small decision, and add them to the program one at a time.
  • Test both sides of every condition, and test the exact boundary values.
  • Storing a comparison like answer.lower() == "yes" in a Boolean makes later conditions read clearly.
  • rides // 3 counts complete groups, which is exactly "one free in every three".
  • Python does and before or. Use parentheses whenever you mix them.

#Make it yours

  • Add a "VIP" rule: anyone whose name is "Ada" rides free. Where in the program does that check have to go?
  • Kids under 5 ride free, though they're almost never 48 inches tall. Add an elif age < 5: branch, and work out where it must go in the chain for it to ever run.
  • Use not to print "Buy a season pass and ride free!" for anyone tall enough who doesn't have one.

What you'll learn

  • Use % and // to test numbers and split amounts into parts.
  • Write if/elif/else chains whose order gives the right answer at every boundary.
  • Build complicated conditions out of small, named Boolean variables.
  • Test every branch of a program, not just the first one that works.

Every exercise this week asks a question and does something different depending on the answer. That means one test run is never enough. Run each program at least once for every branch, plus the boundary values where the answer flips. Save your files in your week3 folder.

#Warm-up

Predict all three lines before you run this:

Five goes into 17 three whole times with 2 left over. Ten divided by 2 leaves no remainder, so the comparison is True. And 3 > 2 is True, which not flips to False.

#Exercise 1: Even or odd

Ask for a whole number and say whether it's even or odd. Test it with 14, 7, 0, and -3.

Need a hint?

What's the remainder when you divide an even number by 2? Which operator gives you a remainder?

Show solution

A number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves nothing over, so number % 2 == 0 is the test. Zero counts as even, and negative numbers work too: in Python, -3 % 2 is 1.

#Exercise 2: Make change

A vending machine owes a customer some cents. Ask how many, then print how many quarters (25¢), dimes (10¢), nickels (5¢), and pennies make that amount, using as few coins as possible.

Need a hint?

cents // 25 tells you how many quarters fit. cents % 25 tells you what's left after taking them out. Store that leftover in a variable, then do the same with 10, then with 5.

Show solution

Each coin follows the same two-step pattern: // counts how many of that coin fit, and % keeps what's left for the next, smaller coin. Reusing the variable left makes the pattern easy to see.

Step through it and watch left shrink from 87 to 12 to 2:

#Exercise 3: Letter grades

Ask for a test score from 0 to 100 and print the letter grade: 90 and up is an A, 80 to 89 a B, 70 to 79 a C, 60 to 69 a D, and below 60 an F.

Test the boundaries: 90, 89, 80, 79, 60, and 59.

Need a hint?

Start with the highest grade and work down. Each elif only runs when every condition above it was False, so by the time you check for a B you already know the score is below 90.

Show solution

The order is what makes this work. You don't need score >= 80 and score < 90 for a B, because a score of 90 or more would already have been caught by the first branch.

Step through it with 79 and count how many conditions Python checks before it finds a match:

#Exercise 4: Log in

The only account has the username coder and the password py4life. Ask for both and print one of three messages:

Need a hint?

Which situation needs both things to be right? Check that one first. A correct username with a wrong password is the next case, and everything else falls to else.

Show solution

The and branch must come first. If you checked username == "coder" on its own first, a correct login would get "Wrong password." The third sample shows that == is case-sensitive: Coder isn't coder.

#Exercise 5: Leap year

A year is a leap year if it's divisible by 4, except that years divisible by 100 aren't, unless they're also divisible by 400. Ask for a year and say whether it's a leap year.

Year Leap year? Why
2024 Yes Divisible by 4
2026 No Not divisible by 4
1900 No Divisible by 100 but not 400
2000 Yes Divisible by 400
Need a hint?

"Divisible by 4" means year % 4 == 0. Store each of the three "divisible by" facts in its own Boolean variable first, then build the condition out of those names. If it helps, follow this chart with each test year:

Show solution

Read the condition aloud: "divisible by 4, and either not divisible by 100 or divisible by 400." The parentheses keep the or together so the code says what the rule says. Run it with all four test years, and make sure each one lands on the answer in the table.

#Exercise 6: Biggest of three

Ask for three numbers (decimals allowed) and print the biggest. Don't use Python's built-in max(); work it out with if, elif, and else.

Make sure it also works when two numbers tie for biggest, like 8, 8, 3, and with negative numbers.

Need a hint?

If a is at least as big as both b and c, you're done. If it isn't, the answer must be whichever of b and c is larger, which takes only one more comparison.

Show solution

If a beats or ties both others, it's the biggest. If not, the answer is whichever of b and c is larger, so the elif only has to compare those two. With 8, 8, 3, the first branch wins and prints 8.0. When two numbers tie for biggest, either one is a correct answer, because they're equal. Trace 3, 5, 8 in your head to see the else branch catch the biggest one.

#Challenge: Rock, paper, scissors

Play one round against the computer. The computer picks at random, the player types a move, and the program announces the result. It should accept Rock or ROCK as well as rock, and reject anything that isn't a real move.

To make the computer choose, put these two lines at the top of your program:

random.choice picks one item from the list in square brackets. You'll learn all about lists in week 5.

Since the computer is random, your runs will differ. Three of the possible outcomes, with the player typing paper each time, plus a typo:

Need a hint?

Make two Boolean variables before any if. valid is true when the move is one of the three words. player_wins is true for the three winning pairs: rock beats scissors, paper beats rock, scissors beats paper. Then the if chain becomes short: invalid, tie, player wins, otherwise the computer wins.

Show solution

Two Boolean variables do the heavy lifting. valid uses or to accept any of the three moves, and not valid catches everything else first. player_wins lists the three winning pairs, each one an and, joined by or. Wrapping a long condition in parentheses lets you split it across lines so it stays readable. After those checks, if it isn't a tie and the player didn't win, the computer must have won, so a plain else is enough. This run's computer move was random, so run it a few times in IDLE to see every outcome.

m5-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Repeat a block of code a set number of times with for and range().
  • Choose the start, stop, and step of range() without falling into the off-by-one trap.
  • Keep a running total or a count while a loop runs.
  • Write a while loop that stops by itself, and rescue a program stuck in one that doesn't.

In the opening of many Simpsons episodes, Bart is stuck at a chalkboard writing the same sentence over and over as punishment. By hand, that takes ages. Python can do it in two lines:

That's five copies. Change 5 to 500, press F5 in IDLE, and Bart's whole afternoon is done before you can blink. This is a loop: code that Python runs again and again. You write the instructions once, and the loop decides how many times they happen.

Python has two loops, and each one answers a different question:

  • for means "do this once for each one of these": each number, each letter, each item.
  • while means "keep doing this as long as something is still true".

#How a for loop is built

Before you look at the output, guess two things: how many Lap lines will print, and which number comes first?

If you guessed four laps starting at 1, you're in good company, and you're off by one. Here's each piece:

  • for lap in creates a loop variable named lap. Each time around, Python puts the next value into it. You pick the name.
  • range(4) hands out the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3. That's four numbers, starting at 0.
  • The colon : at the end of the line says "the loop body comes next".
  • The indented line is the loop body, the part that repeats. IDLE indents it for you after the colon.
  • print("Race over!") isn't indented, so it's not part of the loop. It runs once, after the last lap.

One pass through the body is called an iteration. Step through the program below and watch lap change on each one.

#range() starts at 0 and stops early

Think of the stop number in range() as a finish line you never step on. range(4) runs up to the line and stops right before it, so you get 0 to 3. Give it a second number and you choose where to start. Give it a third and you choose the size of each jump, called the step.

You write Numbers you get Read it as
range(5) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 start at 0, stop before 5
range(1, 6) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 start at 1, stop before 6
range(0, 20, 5) 0, 5, 10, 15 start at 0, add 5 each time, stop before 20
range(10, 0, -3) 10, 7, 4, 1 start at 10, subtract 3 each time, stop before 0

A negative step counts down. Here are two of these in action:

⚠️ Watch out

range(1, 10) gives 1 to 9, not 1 to 10. Getting the last number wrong like this is called an off-by-one error, and professional programmers make it all the time. The fix is the same for everyone: if you want to include the number n, stop at n + 1. So 1 to 10 is range(1, 11).

🧪 Try it yourself

Make a rocket countdown that prints 10, 9, 8 and so on down to 1, then Liftoff!. Which three numbers go inside range()? (Hint: you want to include 1, so where must the countdown stop?)

#A for loop can walk through a string

A string is a row of characters, and for can visit them one at a time. The loop variable holds one letter per iteration. Here's a cheerleader chant that spells out a team name:

The loop ran four times because "CATS" has four characters. You didn't have to count them; the loop stops when it runs out of letters. That's the big advantage of for: it always knows where the end is.

#Keep a running total while you loop

Picture the scorekeeper at a basketball game. The scoreboard starts at 0 before tip-off. Every basket adds points to whatever's already up there. Nobody resets the board after each shot. That's the accumulator pattern:

  1. Before the loop, create a variable that starts at 0.
  2. Inside the loop, add the new value to it.
  3. After the loop, the variable holds the total.

This program asks how long you practiced on three days. The run below shows what happens when someone types 20, 35, and 15:

The key line is total = total + minutes. Read it right to left: take the old total, add the new minutes, and store the answer back in total.

A counter is the same pattern, except you add 1 instead of a value, and usually only when an if says so. This one counts how many numbers from 1 to 10 divide evenly by 3. Step through it and watch count sit still most of the time and jump only when n % 3 == 0.

Here's the classic accumulator bug. The total is set to 0 inside the loop, so the scoreboard gets wiped before every shot:

There's no error message, just a wrong answer: 15 minutes instead of 70. Only the last day survives, because each pass starts over from zero. Move total = 0 above the loop and it's fixed.

#while: keep going as long as something is true

A for loop is like a playlist with a set number of songs. A while loop is "keep the music playing until someone says stop". You don't know in advance how many songs that will be.

Python checks the condition first. If it's True, the body runs, and then Python goes back and checks again. The moment the condition is False, Python skips past the loop.

The line that makes this work is fuel = fuel - 1. Every iteration moves fuel one step closer to 0, so fuel > 0 is guaranteed to become False eventually. Every while loop needs a line like that, something in the body that pushes the condition toward False.

#Ask again until the answer makes sense

while shines when you can't know ahead of time how many repeats you'll need. You can't predict how many times a user will type nonsense, so you keep asking until they don't. In this run, the user typed 200, then -3, then 13:

The input() line appears twice: once before the loop, so age has a value to check, and once inside, so the user gets another chance. Leave out the one inside and the loop asks nothing new, so a bad answer keeps it spinning forever.

#Leave early with break

Sometimes it's simpler to write while True:, a loop that would run forever on its own, and jump out with break when something happens. break ends the nearest loop immediately, even in the middle of the body.

Notice that stop didn't get counted. When break runs, Python leaves the loop on the spot, so count = count + 1 never happens for that word.

#When a loop never stops

If nothing in the body ever makes the condition False, you get an infinite loop. This version forgot to subtract from fuel, so it prints Fuel left: 3 forever:

💡 Tip

To stop a runaway program in IDLE, click in the Shell window and press Ctrl+C (on a Mac too, it's Control, not Command), or choose Shell > Interrupt Execution. You'll see KeyboardInterrupt and a fresh >>> prompt. Then look for the variable your loop forgot to update.

#for or while?

Ask yourself one question: do I know how many times this should repeat?

Situation Loop Why
Print a times table from 1 to 12 for You know it's 12 rows.
Go through every letter of a word for The word knows its own length.
Ask for a password until it's right while It might take one try or ten.
Roll a die until you get a 6 while Nobody knows when the 6 shows up.

If you can count the repeats before the loop starts, use for. If the loop is waiting for something to happen, use while.

#Mistakes everyone makes with loops

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting the colon. for lap in range(4) with no : at the end stops the program before it starts, with SyntaxError: expected ':'. IDLE highlights the spot in red.

Indenting the wrong lines. Only indented lines repeat. If a line you meant to repeat isn't indented, it runs once, after the loop. If a line you meant to run once is indented, it repeats every time. In IDLE, select lines and use Format > Indent Region or Format > Dedent Region to move them in or out together.

Here's the missing-colon error for real, so you'll recognize it:

Check your understanding

4 questions

1What numbers does range(2, 8, 2) give you?

  • The stop number is never included, so 8 is left out.

  • Start at 2, jump by 2, and stop before reaching 8.

  • That's range(2, 8). The third number changes the step to 2.

  • The first number sets the start, so it begins at 2, not 0.

Show answer

B. Start at 2, jump by 2, and stop before reaching 8.

2A loop runs for n in range(1, 4):, and its body is total = 0 followed by total = total + n. After the loop, print(total) runs. What does it print?

  • That's the goal, but total is wiped back to 0 at the start of every pass.

  • Each pass resets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 3, survives.

  • The reset happens before the add on each pass, so the last pass leaves 0 + 3.

  • total is created inside the loop before it's used, so Python never complains. It's a logic error, not a crash.

Show answer

B. Each pass resets total to 0 and then adds n, so only the last value, 3, survives.

3You want to keep asking "Play again? (y/n)" until the user types n. Which loop fits best?

  • That asks exactly 10 times, even if the user typed n on the first try.

  • You can't know how many rounds someone will want, so you repeat until they say stop.

  • That loops once over the single letter n, which has nothing to do with what the user types.

Show answer

B. You can't know how many rounds someone will want, so you repeat until they say stop.

4A program sets count = 10, then runs while count > 0: with just print(count) in the body. What happens?

  • Nothing in the body changes count, so it stays 10.

  • count > 0 is always True. The body needs count = count - 1.

  • The condition is True at the start (10 > 0), so the body does run, again and again.

Show answer

B. count > 0 is always True. The body needs count = count - 1.

Key takeaways

  • for repeats once for each value it's given: each number from range(), or each letter in a string.
  • range(stop) starts at 0 and stops before stop. To include n, stop at n + 1.
  • Only the indented lines under for or while repeat.
  • A running total starts at 0 before the loop and grows inside it.
  • A while loop needs a line in its body that moves the condition toward False, or a break.
  • Stuck in an infinite loop in IDLE? Press Ctrl+C in the Shell window.
