What you'll learn

  • Build a complete game in five small steps, running it after each one.
  • Use a while loop that repeats until the player wins or runs out of tries.
  • Count tries with a counter, and stop the loop with two conditions joined by and.
  • Pick a secret with random.randint(), and make it repeatable while you test.

The computer picks a secret number from 1 to 100. You guess, and it says "too high" or "too low" until you nail it or run out of tries. It's about 25 lines long, and it uses almost everything from the first four weeks: variables, input(), int(), if/elif/else, and, and this week's while loop.

Here's the plan for the finished game. Every box on this chart becomes a line or two of code.

We'll build it in five steps. In IDLE, choose File > New File, save it as guess.py, and press F5 after every step. Don't skip ahead. If something breaks, the bug is almost certainly in the few lines you just added.

#Step 1: One guess, with a fixed secret

A random secret is a pain while you're building, because you never know the right answer to type. So programmers hard-code it: they pick a number themselves, get everything working, and switch to random at the very end.

The comparison works. Try it with 60 and with 42 so you see all three branches. The problem is obvious, though: you get exactly one chance, and then the program ends.

#Step 2: Keep asking until the guess is right

We want to repeat "ask, then compare" until the guess matches. Nobody knows how many guesses that will take, which is the signal to use while. In this run the player guesses 50, then 25, then 42:

Look at guess = 0 before the loop. The while line is the very first thing to check guess, before the player has typed anything, so guess has to exist already. Starting at 0 is safe because 0 can never be the secret. Here's what happens if you leave that line out:

Read the last line first: NameError: name 'guess' is not defined. Python is saying "you asked me about guess, but I've never heard of it." The line number points straight at the while.

💡 Tip

Everything that should repeat (the asking and the comparing) must be indented under while. If you accidentally un-indent the if block, the game asks over and over but never gives a hint, because the hints only run after the loop ends.

#Step 3: Count the tries

Players want to know how well they did. That's a counter: start at 0 before the loop, and add 1 every time the loop body runs.

Step through the same game below. Watch guess and tries change together, and notice the exact moment the while condition turns False.

#Step 4: Add a limit so you can lose

A game you can't lose isn't much of a game. We'll stop after max_tries guesses. Now the loop should keep going only while both of these are true: the guess is wrong and there are tries left. That's and from last week.

guess != secret tries < max_tries Keep looping?
True (still wrong) True (tries left) Yes
False (correct!) True No, the player won
True (still wrong) False (out of tries) No, the player lost

Here's the code, tested on purpose with a losing game, because the losing path is the one you're most likely to forget to check:

The loop can now end for two different reasons, so the if after it works out which one happened. If the last guess still doesn't match, the only other way out was running out of tries.

#Step 5: Make the secret random

Python comes with a toolbox called the random module. The line import random at the top of your file opens it up, and random.randint(1, 100) hands you a whole number from 1 to 100. Unlike range(), both ends are included, so 100 can come up.

That brings back the testing problem. How do you check the game works when you don't know the answer? Here's a useful secret about computer randomness: it isn't truly random. Python generates its "random" numbers from a formula that begins at a starting value called the seed. Give it the same seed and you get the same numbers every time. So while testing, we add random.seed(2026), which makes the secret come out the same on every run.

Here's the finished game. The player in this run uses the smart strategy from the tip below:

Once it works, delete the random.seed(2026) line (or put # in front of it to turn it into a comment). Now every game has a new secret, and even you don't know it.

💡 Tip

Seven tries is always enough if you play smart. Guess the middle (50). If that's too high, guess the middle of what's left (25), and keep cutting the range in half. After 7 halvings, 100 possible numbers shrink to 1. That strategy is called binary search, and it's how computers find things fast.

#What can go wrong

The player types a word. int() only understands digits, so fifty crashes the game:

The last line, ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'fifty', is int() saying it can't turn that text into a number. In Week 6 you'll write a function that keeps asking until it gets a real number.

Forgetting tries = tries + 1. The counter never moves, tries < max_tries stays True forever, and the limit never kicks in. You can only lose by guessing wrong forever.

Putting secret = random.randint(1, 100) inside the loop. The secret changes after every guess, so "too low" followed by "too high" stops making any sense.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the game set guess = 0 before the while loop?

  • The player's guess replaces it on the very first pass, so 0 is never used as a real guess.

  • The condition guess != secret runs first, so guess must already exist, and 0 can never be the secret.

  • There's only one game per run here. It's about giving the condition something to check.

Show answer

B. The condition guess != secret runs first, so guess must already exist, and 0 can never be the secret.

2max_tries is 5. The player's fifth guess is wrong. What happens next?

  • After the fifth guess, tries < max_tries is 5 < 5, which is False, so the loop stops.

  • The and needs both parts to be True. With no tries left the loop stops, and guess != secret is still True, so the loss message prints.

  • Nothing is wrong with the code; running out of tries is a normal way for the loop to finish.

Show answer

B. The and needs both parts to be True. With no tries left the loop stops, and guess != secret is still True, so the loss message prints.

3Why is random.randint(1, 100) above the loop and not inside it?

  • Inside the loop, a new secret would be picked after every guess, and the hints would point at a moving target.

  • random.randint() works anywhere. The problem is when it runs, not where it's allowed.

  • Speed isn't the issue. Picking a new secret every turn would make the game impossible to win on purpose.

Show answer

A. Inside the loop, a new secret would be picked after every guess, and the hints would point at a moving target.

Key takeaways

  • Build in small steps and run after each one, so every bug is in the last few lines you wrote.
  • Hard-code values like the secret while you build, then make them random at the end.
  • A while loop is the right choice when you can't know how many times it will repeat.
  • A counter starts at 0 before the loop and goes up by 1 inside it.
  • and lets a loop stop for more than one reason; an if after the loop can tell which reason it was.
  • random.randint(a, b) includes both a and b. random.seed() makes "random" results repeatable for testing.

#Make it yours

Pick one or more:

  1. Ask the player to choose easy (1 to 10), medium (1 to 50), or hard (1 to 100), and use their choice in randint. Don't forget the welcome message should match.
  2. When a guess is within 5 of the secret, print So close! along with the hint. You'll need to work out the distance with secret - guess and check both directions.
  3. Wrap the whole game in another while loop that asks Play again? (y/n) at the end, and print the player's best (lowest) number of tries when they quit.

  • Invent Your Own Computer Games with Python, Chapter 3: Guess the Number (opens in a new tab): a free book chapter that builds the same game a different way and explains each line.

What you'll learn

  • Pick the right range() for a counting job on the first try.
  • Use the accumulator and counter patterns without resetting them by mistake.
  • Write while loops that stop for the right reason, including after a set number of tries.
  • Combine loops with if and string tricks to draw a pattern.

Loops click through repetition, which is fitting. Make a new IDLE file for each exercise, run it, and compare what you see with the sample output. Open a hint only after a real attempt, and the solution only after the hint. Ten minutes of being stuck teaches you more than ten seconds of reading an answer.

When a loop misbehaves, add a print() inside the body that shows your variables, like print("i is", i, "total is", total). Watching the values change one iteration at a time usually exposes the bug in seconds. Delete the extra line once it's fixed.

#Warm-up: predict the last number

Read this program and decide what the final line prints before you step through it. Hint: x triples every pass.

Did you say 27? Lots of people do. The loop checks x < 50 only at the top of each pass. When x is 27, the check passes, and the body triples it to 81 before Python checks again. A while loop can overshoot its target, because the condition is tested before the body runs, not after.

#Exercise 1: Cheer squad

Print the even numbers from 2 to 20, one per line, and then print Who do we appreciate?. Use one range() with three numbers and no if.

Need a hint?

The third number in range() is how far to jump each time. Where should you start, how far should you jump, and what stop number makes sure 20 is included?

Show solution

Start at 2, jump by 2, and stop before 21 so 20 makes it in.

The last print isn't indented, so it runs once after the loop ends. range(2, 20, 2) would stop at 18.

#Exercise 2: Times table

Ask the user for a number and print its times table from 1 to 10.

Need a hint?

The number the user types stays the same the whole time. What changes on each line is the number you multiply it by, so that's the loop variable. Remember int(), because input() gives you text.

Show solution

range(1, 11) gives 1 through 10. A common slip is range(10), which starts at 0 and ends at 9, so your table would start with 7 x 0 = 0 and miss 7 x 10.

#Exercise 3: Add it all up

Ask for a number n and print the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n. There's a story that a young Carl Friedrich Gauss, later a famous mathematician, was told by his teacher to add 1 to 100 and finished almost instantly. Your loop will be even faster. Check that 100 gives 5050.

Need a hint?

This is the accumulator pattern from the notes. You need a variable that starts at 0 before the loop. Then think hard about the stop number: does your range() include n itself?

Show solution

We stop at n + 1 because range never includes its stop number. With range(1, n) you'd get 4950, since 100 itself would be left out. That's the off-by-one error in the wild.

#Exercise 4: Three strikes

The secret password is tacocat. Keep asking until the user types it or has tried 3 times. Print Wrong password. after each wrong try. At the end, print Access granted. or Locked out. Try again later.

Need a hint?

This loop has two reasons to stop, just like the guessing game: a correct password, or running out of tries. Join the two "keep going" conditions with and. After the loop, check which reason it was.

Show solution

Tacocat is rejected because string comparisons care about capital letters. entry = "" before the loop gives entry a starting value that can't be the password. Here's the same program with three wrong tries, to check the other ending:

#Exercise 5: Savings goal

You want to save up for something. Ask for the goal and how much you save each week (both can have decimals, so use float()). Use a while loop to add one week of savings at a time, print the running total each week, and finish by saying how many weeks it took.

Need a hint?

You need two variables that change every pass: the money saved so far and the number of weeks. What condition should keep the loop going? Think "not there yet".

Show solution

while fits because nobody knows the number of weeks in advance. One more thing to think about: what happens if someone types 0 for the weekly amount? saved never grows, so saved < goal is True forever. That's an infinite loop (Ctrl+C to escape). Can you add an if before the loop that catches it and prints a polite message instead?

#Exercise 6: Vowel counter

Ask for a word and count its vowels, capital or lowercase. You'll need a for loop over the string, plus one new trick: letter in "aeiouAEIOU" is True when letter is one of those characters.

Need a hint?

Loop over the word one letter at a time. Inside the loop, an if decides whether this letter deserves a point. That makes it a counter, so where does vowels = 0 belong?

Show solution

On each pass, letter holds one character: E, then d, then u, and so on. The counter only goes up when the if is True. Without the capitals in "aeiouAEIOU", the capital E wouldn't count and you'd get 4.

#Before the challenge: strings can be multiplied

Multiplying a string by a whole number repeats it. "*" * 3 is "***", and " " * 2 is two spaces. Put that inside a loop and the loop variable controls how long each line is. Step through this staircase and watch the line grow:

#Challenge: Star pyramid

Ask for a height and print a centered pyramid of stars, like this:

For a height of 4, here's what each row needs. Your job is to find the rule that turns row into these numbers.

Row Spaces in front Stars
1 3 1
2 2 3
3 1 5
4 0 7
Need a hint?

Each row has 2 more stars than the one before, starting from 1. Try doubling the row number and adjusting. The spaces go down by one each row and end at 0 on the last row, so they depend on both height and row.

Show solution

Row row (counting from 1) has 2 * row - 1 stars, with height - row spaces in front of them.

Want more? Flip the pyramid upside down by counting row down with range(height, 0, -1). Or ask for the character to draw with, so the pyramid can be made of # or @.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a list and read any item from it by its index, including from the end.
  • Explain why the first index is 0, and fix an IndexError when you go too far.
  • Add, change, and remove items with append, insert, remove, and pop.
  • Loop over a list to total, count, or print it, and change every item in place.

Say you're tracking quiz scores for a class of 25. With what you know so far, that's 25 variables: score1, score2, all the way to score25. The average is one enormous line adding all 25 names together. Then a new student joins, and every line that mentions the scores has to change.

A list solves this. It's one variable that holds many values, in order. Add a 26th score and the list just gets longer; the code that averages it doesn't change at all.

#Making a list

Put the items inside square brackets, with commas between them:

Printing the whole list shows the brackets and quotes, which is handy for checking what's inside. snacks[0] reaches in and pulls out one item. len(snacks) counts the items: 4.

A list can hold strings, numbers, Booleans, or a mix, like [16, "Maya", True]. Most of the time, though, every item is the same kind of thing. [] is an empty list, a container with nothing in it yet.

#Why the first index is 0

Every item has a position number called its index, and Python starts counting at 0. That looks strange until you think of the index as how many steps from the front an item is. The first item is zero steps from the front. The second is one step away.

Index 0 1 2 3
Item "chips" "apples" "popcorn" "pretzels"
Negative index -4 -3 -2 -1
  • snacks[0] is the first item.
  • snacks[-1] is the last item, however long the list is. snacks[-2] is second to last.
  • The last index is always len(snacks) - 1, here 3. There are 4 items, but the numbering started at 0.

#What happens when you go too far

Before you look: this list has three items. What will snacks[3] give you?

Three snacks means indexes 0, 1, and 2. Index 3 would be a fourth item, and there isn't one. When you see IndexError: list index out of range, your first suspect should be counting from 1 instead of 0. The ~~~^^^ marks under the code point at the part of the line that went wrong: the index. (On your computer the traceback shows the full path to your file instead of main.py.)

#Changing a list

Strings can't be changed once they're made, but lists can. You can swap, add, and remove items whenever you like. These are the moves you'll use most:

Code What it does
snacks[1] = "grapes" replace the item at index 1
snacks.append("cookies") add to the end
snacks.insert(0, "carrots") add at index 0, and shift everything else along
snacks.remove("chips") remove the first "chips" it finds
snacks.pop() remove the last item and hand it back to you
snacks.pop(1) remove the item at index 1 and hand it back
"popcorn" in snacks True if that item is in the list

The dot in snacks.append(...) means "this list, do this". The action belongs to the list, so you write the list's name first. Step through these changes and watch the list on the right after each line:

Two things to notice. After insert(0, ...), every item moved one place to the right, so "chips" went from index 0 to index 1. And pop() didn't just delete "cookies", it handed it back so we could store it in last.

remove has a catch: it crashes if the item isn't in the list.

⚠️ Watch out

ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list means you asked to remove something that isn't there. Guard it with in on the line before: if "pizza" in snacks:, then indent the remove under it.

#Looping over a list

Here's where lists pay off. A for loop hands you each item in turn, so you never need to know how many there are:

The average divides by len(scores), not by the number 5. Add a sixth score to the first line and every result is still correct, with nothing else to edit. That's the payoff from the opening example.

Python also has built-in sum(), max(), and min() for lists of numbers. They do the same job as the total loop. It's still worth writing the loop yourself at least once, because next time you need something those three don't do (like counting scores above 90), you'll know how to build it.

#Looping with indexes

Sometimes you want the position as well as the item, for example to print a numbered list. range(len(chores)) produces every valid index, from 0 up to the last one:

People count from 1, so we print i + 1. Behind the scenes Python is still using 0, 1, 2.

#Changing every item: the copy trap

This one catches almost everyone. Both loops below are supposed to double every price. Predict what prices holds after each loop, then step through and check.

In the first loop, price gets a copy of each value. Doubling the copy changes price, and the list never hears about it. You can see price change in the trace while prices stays the same. To change the list itself, you have to assign to a spot in the list, prices[i] = ..., and that means looping over the indexes.

#Building a list as you go

Lists often start empty and fill up while the program runs. This one keeps asking for names until the user presses Enter without typing anything, which gives input() an empty string, "". In this run the user typed three names and then pressed Enter on a blank line:

It's the "ask again" while loop from Week 4 with one new line, friends.append(name), that saves each answer before asking for the next.

#Mistakes to watch for

⚠️ Watch out

Off by one at the end. The last item is my_list[len(my_list) - 1] or simply my_list[-1]. my_list[len(my_list)] is always one past the end and gives IndexError.

Round brackets instead of square. snacks(0) gives TypeError: 'list' object is not callable, because round brackets mean "call this like a function". Use snacks[0].

Forgetting the dot. It's snacks.append("x"), not append(snacks, "x"), which gives a NameError.

Changing the loop variable and expecting the list to change. Use my_list[i] = ... inside a for i in range(len(my_list)) loop.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1colors = ["red", "green", "blue", "gold"]. What is colors[-2]?

  • That's colors[1]. Negative indexes count from the end, starting at -1.

  • -1 is the last item ("gold"), so -2 is the one just before it.

  • That's colors[-1], the very last item.

  • Negative indexes are allowed, as long as you don't go past the front. -2 is fine for a 4-item list.

Show answer

B. -1 is the last item ("gold"), so -2 is the one just before it.

2nums = [5, 10, 15], then nums.append(20) and nums.pop(0). What's in nums now?

  • append added 20 and pop(0) removed the first item, so the list did change.

  • That's after the append. pop(0) then removes the item at index 0.

  • 20 goes on the end, then the item at index 0, which is 5, is removed.

  • pop hands back the removed item, but nothing here prints it. And the removed item was 5, not 20.

Show answer

C. 20 goes on the end, then the item at index 0, which is 5, is removed.

3You want to add 1 point to every score in scores. Which loop actually changes the list?

  • s is a copy of each item. Changing it leaves the list exactly as it was.

  • Assigning to scores[i] writes the new value back into the list itself.

  • Here i is each score, not each index, so scores[88] would crash with IndexError.

Show answer

B. Assigning to scores[i] writes the new value back into the list itself.

4A list has 6 items. What is its last valid index?

  • The indexes start at 0, so 6 would be a seventh item.

  • Six items are numbered 0 through 5. The last index is always len - 1.

  • That's two past the end. Python would answer with IndexError.

Show answer

B. Six items are numbered 0 through 5. The last index is always len - 1.

Key takeaways

  • A list is one variable holding many values in order: scores = [88, 92, 75].
  • Indexes start at 0 (steps from the front). [-1] is the last item, and the last index is len(list) - 1.
  • append adds to the end, insert adds anywhere, remove deletes by value, and pop deletes by position and hands the item back.
  • for item in my_list: visits every item. Use len() instead of typing the count, so the code still works when the list grows.
  • To change items in place, loop over indexes and assign to my_list[i].

#Further reading

  • Python Tutorial: Lists (opens in a new tab): the official introduction to making, indexing, and changing lists.
  • Python Tutorial: More on Lists (opens in a new tab): every list method in one short table, with examples.
  • Automate the Boring Stuff, Chapter 4: Lists (opens in a new tab): a free book chapter that goes a little further, with lots of small programs.

What you'll learn

  • Build a menu-driven program that keeps running until the user quits.
  • Store tasks in a list and add, show, and remove them as the user asks.
  • Translate between the numbers people see (1, 2, 3) and Python's indexes (0, 1, 2).
  • Check a number is in range before using it as an index, so the app can't crash on a bad task number.

Every to-do app on your phone, from Google Tasks to Apple Reminders, is built around the same idea as a Python list: an ordered row of items you can add to, read, and remove from. Today you'll build a small one that runs in the IDLE Shell. It shows a menu, the user types a letter, the program changes the list to match, and when they quit it reports what they got done.

This is the shape of the finished program. The whole app lives inside one loop that only ends when the user types q.

Create a new file in IDLE and save it as todo.py. You'll use a list, append, pop, len(), indexes, for loops, and a while True loop with break.

#Step 1: Show a list with numbers

Start with three tasks already in the list, so there's something to look at:

range(len(tasks)) gives the indexes 0, 1, 2, and we print i + 1 because people count from 1. Hold on to that idea: in Step 4, the user will type a number they see, and you'll have to turn it back into an index.

#Step 2: A menu that keeps coming back

An app should keep running until the user decides to stop. while True repeats forever, and break gets us out when the user types q. Replace everything in your file with this. The run below tests all three paths: adding a task, a wrong letter, and quitting.

print() with nothing inside prints a blank line, which keeps each menu from running into the last one. The list now starts empty ([]) and grows with append.

Why while True with a break, instead of a condition like while choice != "q"? Because the program has to ask before it can know whether to stop, and the question is in the middle of the loop. while True says "keep going", and break stops the loop right at the moment the answer comes in.

💡 Tip

Always include an else for "none of the above". Without it, a typo like x does nothing at all, and the user can't tell whether the app is broken or just waiting.

#Step 3: Show the tasks

Add a new branch for s. If the list is empty, a friendly message beats printing nothing. Put this just above elif choice == "q"::

Watch the indentation. The elif lines up with if choice == "a":, the for sits inside the else, and the print sits inside the for. That's three levels deep. Update the menu line to "a = add, s = show, q = quit" too. Here's the whole file so far, tested with an s before anything's been added, then an add, then another s:

#Step 4: Check off a task

To remove a task by its position, use pop with an index. tasks.pop(1) removes the item at index 1 and hands it back, so you can print it. Before adding it to the app, try the idea on its own. Step through and watch the list close up the gap:

The user sees task 2, but Python stores it at index 1. That's why we pop(number - 1). And after the pop, "practice piano" slid from index 2 to index 1, so it would show up as task 2 next time.

There's one more danger: tasks.pop(7) on a three-item list crashes with IndexError. So we check that the number is between 1 and the length of the list before popping. Add this branch next to the others:

#Step 5: Keep score and say goodbye

A second list, done, collects finished tasks. Each time you pop from tasks, append the same item to done. When the user quits, loop over done to show what they got through. Here's the finished program, with a full test run: three tasks added, the list shown, task 2 finished, a task number that doesn't exist, the list shown again, and quit.

Look at the second s in the output. After feed the cat was popped, practice piano moved up from number 3 to number 2. The list closed the gap, exactly like the trace in Step 4. And task number 7 got a polite message instead of a crash, thanks to the range check.

#Try to break it

Testers earn their pay by doing what users aren't supposed to do. Try each of these and predict the result first:

  • Type s before adding anything. You should see Nothing to do. Nice!.
  • Type d, then 0, then try d again with -1. The range check should catch both, since neither is between 1 and the list's length.
  • Type d, then two. This one crashes with ValueError, because int() can't convert a word. Next week you'll write a function that keeps asking until it gets a real number, and it will slot straight into this app.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1The user types 3 to finish their third task. Why does the code call tasks.pop(number - 1)?

  • pop(i) removes exactly the item at index i. The - 1 is about how people count.

  • Task 3 on screen is stored at index 2, so we subtract 1 to translate.

  • Subtracting 1 changes which index is used, not how many items stay.

Show answer

B. Task 3 on screen is stored at index 2, so we subtract 1 to translate.

2What would happen without the check number >= 1 and number <= len(tasks)?

  • pop doesn't ignore them. Asking for an index past the end crashes.

  • tasks.pop(6) on a 3-item list has nowhere to look. The check catches it and prints a message instead.

  • Only pop() with no index removes the last item. A bad index is an error.

Show answer

B. tasks.pop(6) on a 3-item list has nowhere to look. The check catches it and prints a message instead.

3Why is the whole app inside while True with a break, rather than a loop that runs a fixed number of times?

  • while True keeps the menu coming back as long as needed, and break ends it the moment the user types q.

  • They can. The problem is that a for loop needs to know how many times to run.

  • Many programs use input() without break. Here it's simply the cleanest way to stop a menu loop.

Show answer

A. while True keeps the menu coming back as long as needed, and break ends it the moment the user types q.

Key takeaways

  • A menu app is a while True loop: show the choices, read one, act on it, and break on quit.
  • Give every menu an else so wrong input gets a helpful message.
  • People count from 1, Python from 0: show i + 1, and use number - 1 to turn a typed number back into an index.
  • pop(index) removes an item and hands it back, and the items after it shift down to fill the gap.
  • Check a number is in range before using it as an index.

#Make it yours

  1. You finished 1 tasks reads oddly. Use an if to print task when there's exactly one.
  2. Add c for "clear", which empties the whole list. Try tasks = [] first, then look up tasks.clear() in the docs below.
  3. Refuse to add the same task twice: check if task in tasks: before you append, and tell the user it's already there.
  4. Let the user add several tasks in a row with a, stopping when they press Enter on a blank line. (You built that loop in the notes for this week.)

  • Python for Everybody: Lists (opens in a new tab): free lecture videos and exercises on lists from a university course.

What you'll learn

  • Read items by positive and negative index, and use len() instead of typing counts.
  • Track a total, a count, and a "biggest so far" while looping over a list.
  • Build a list from user input, then loop over it a second time.
  • Change every item in place, search with a flag variable, and use one loop inside another.

Each exercise below uses this week's list skills on a new problem. Type each one yourself instead of pasting; typing is how your fingers learn where the square brackets and colons go. If a list isn't doing what you expect, print() the whole list partway through your program. Seeing [71.0, 80.5, 64.0] tells you far more than guessing.

#Warm-up: track the list in your head

Before you step through this, write down what you think the last line prints: the list and its length.

The trick is line 3. letters[0] is read before anything is removed, so "a" gets copied onto the end. Then pop(0) removes the original "a" from the front, and everything shifts left by one.

#Exercise 1: Favorite foods

Make a list of your three favorite foods. Print the first one, the last one (using a negative index), and how many foods are in the list.

Need a hint?

The first item is at index 0. For the last item, there's an index that works no matter how long the list is. len() does the counting.

Show solution

foods[-1] still gives the last item if you add a fourth food later. foods[2] wouldn't, because the fourth food would be at index 3.

#Exercise 2: Receipt

You have prices = [4.50, 12.00, 3.25, 8.75]. Using one loop, and without sum() or max(), work out the total and the most expensive item.

Need a hint?

You need two variables that update on every pass. The total starts at 0. For the most expensive, start with a price you know is in the list, then replace it whenever you find a bigger one.

Show solution

biggest starts as the first price, and the loop replaces it whenever something larger comes along.

Why not start biggest at 0? Here it would work, but if every value were negative (winter temperatures, say), 0 would wrongly "win". Starting with a real item from the list is always safe.

#Exercise 3: Who passed?

Given scores = [72, 55, 90, 68, 100, 70, 43], count how many scores are 70 or higher and print the sentence below. Don't type the 7 yourself; let Python count the list.

Need a hint?

It's a counter with an if inside the loop. Look closely at "70 or higher": which comparison operator includes 70 itself?

Show solution

With > instead of >=, the student with exactly 70 would fail, and you'd print 3. Boundaries are where bugs hide, which is why the list includes a 70.

#Exercise 4: Weather report

Ask for five daily high temperatures (they can have decimals) and store them in a list. Then print the list, the average rounded to 1 decimal place, the hottest temperature, and how many days were above average.

Need a hint?

Start with an empty list and append each temperature inside a for loop over range(1, 6). You can't know which days are above average until you've collected all five, so you'll need a second loop after the first one.

Show solution

The first loop collects, and the second loop compares. Notice the list shows 71.0 even though the user typed 71: float() turns every answer into a decimal number.

#Exercise 5: Ten percent off

A store is having a sale. Change every price in prices = [20.0, 15.0, 9.99, 42.5] to 90% of what it was, rounded to 2 decimal places. You must change the list itself, not just print new numbers.

Need a hint?

Remember the copy trap from the notes. To write a new value back into the list, you need to know where in the list it goes, so loop over the indexes.

Show solution

If you wrote for price in prices: with price = price * 0.9 inside, the list didn't change, because that loop only updates a copy. Assigning to prices[i] is what changes the list.

#Exercise 6: Find your spot in line

lineup = ["Ava", "Ben", "Chloe", "Dev", "Eli"]. Ask for a name. If it's in the list, print its position counting from 1. If not, say so.

Need a hint?

Loop over the indexes and compare each name. The tricky part is the "not in line" message: you can only know nobody matched after checking everyone. Use a variable that starts as False and flips to True when you find a match.

Show solution

A flag variable remembers whether something happened during the loop.

And with a name that isn't there:

The "not in line" message has to come after the loop. If you put it in an else inside the loop, it would print once for every name that doesn't match: four times for Chloe.

#Before the challenge: a loop inside a loop

The challenge needs one loop inside another. The rule is simple once you see it: the inner loop runs all the way through for every single pass of the outer loop. Step through this and count how many times the inner print runs.

Two teams times three players makes six lines. Any variable you want to start fresh for each outer pass (like a counter) must be set inside the outer loop, just above the inner one.

#Challenge: Lunch vote

The class voted on a party lunch:

  1. Build a new list unique with each option only once, in the order it first appears.
  2. Print how many repeat votes were left out.
  3. Print how many votes each option got.
Need a hint?

For part 1, not in is the opposite of in: only append a vote if it isn't in unique yet. For part 3, the outer loop goes over unique, and the inner loop goes over every vote and counts the ones that match. Where does the counter reset?

Show solution

The outer loop picks one option, and the inner loop counts it through the whole votes list. count = 0 sits inside the outer loop so every option starts counting from zero. (Put it above both loops and the counts pile up: 3, 5, 6, 7.) Lists also have a shortcut, votes.count("pizza"), and now you know what it's doing behind the scenes.

Polish idea: sushi got 1 votes isn't quite English. An if count == 1: can fix it.

What you'll learn

  • Define a function with def and call it as many times as you like.
  • Pass information in with parameters, and hand an answer back with return.
  • Tell print and return apart, and explain where a None came from.
  • Read a traceback from the bottom up to find what went wrong, where, and how the program got there.

Your quiz program prints a banner of ===== lines with a title at the start, between rounds, and at the end. That's the same four lines pasted into three places. Then your friend says the banner should use ***** instead. Now you're editing three places, and you'll almost certainly miss one.

A function fixes this. You write the lines once, give them a name, and run them by name whenever you want. Change the function and every place that uses it changes too. You've been using functions since Week 1: print(), input(), len(), and int() are all functions someone else wrote. This week you write your own.

#Define it once, call it anywhere

  • def means "define". It's followed by the function's name, parentheses, and a colon.
  • The indented lines underneath are the function body.
  • Defining a function doesn't run it. Python reads the body, remembers it under the name cheer, and moves on. The body only runs when you call the function by writing cheer().

That's why Before the game prints first, even though the def is at the top. Step through it and watch the call stack on the right: each time cheer() is called, a new cheer() box appears on top of the global one, and it disappears when the function finishes.

Python runs your file from top to bottom, so a function has to be defined above the first line that calls it. Call it too early and Python has never heard of it:

#Parameters: give the function something to work with

Think of a function as a form with blanks: "Hi ____!" A parameter is the blank, a variable in the parentheses of the def line. The value you fill in when you call the function is called an argument.

Arguments match parameters by position: the first argument goes into name, and the second goes into smiles. Swap them, greet(3, "Luis"), and Python tries to add "Hi " to the number 3. Leave one out and Python stops before the function even starts:

The message names the function, says how many arguments are missing, and even tells you which parameter didn't get a value.

#return: hand an answer back

print and return both seem to "give you the answer", but they're very different. print is like shouting the answer across the room: everyone hears it, but nobody wrote it down. return is like handing the answer on a sticky note to whoever asked, so they can keep it, do math with it, or pass it on.

rectangle_area(4, 5) is replaced by the value it returns, 20, and that value is stored in room. When Python reaches return, the function ends right there. Any lines after it in the body are skipped.

#print and return, side by side

This is the most common confusion with functions. Predict what x and y will be before you look:

add_print shows 5 on the screen but hands nothing back, so x is None, Python's word for "no value". add_return hands back 5, and y keeps it. The rule: if you need to use the answer later, return it.

Functions can return any type, including True and False. That makes if statements read almost like English:

#Variables inside a function stay inside

42 prints fine, and then Python crashes on the last line. answer is a local variable: it's created when double starts and thrown away when double finishes. Code outside the function can't see it. To use a function's result outside, return it and store it: result = double(21).

#Reading error messages

Red text in the Shell isn't Python being rude. It's a detailed report on exactly what went wrong and where, called a traceback. Here's a program where the crash happens two function calls deep:

Read a traceback from the bottom up:

  1. The last line says what happened. ZeroDivisionError: division by zero.
  2. The lines just above it say where. Line 2, inside average.
  3. Further up shows how you got there. Line 8 called report, and line 5, inside report, called average.

Maya's line ran fine, which tells you the code works in general and something about Luis's input is unusual: his list is empty, so len(scores) is 0. Step through the program to watch the call stack grow to three boxes deep, exactly matching the three File lines in the traceback, right before it crashes:

#Error types you'll meet

Error Example message Usual cause
SyntaxError '(' was never closed or expected ':' a missing bracket, quote, or colon
IndentationError expected an indented block after 'for' statement on line 1 the body under if, for, or def isn't indented
NameError name 'scroe' is not defined. Did you mean: 'score'? a typo, or using a variable or function before it exists
TypeError can only concatenate str (not "int") to str mixing types, like "You are " + 13. Use str(13) or an f-string.
TypeError greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'smiles' calling a function with too few arguments
ValueError invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twelve' the right type with an impossible value, like int("twelve")
IndexError list index out of range asking for colors[2] when the list has only 2 items
ZeroDivisionError division by zero dividing by a variable that turned out to be 0

💡 Tip

In IDLE, a SyntaxError or IndentationError appears in a pop-up box titled SyntaxError before your program even starts, and IDLE marks the problem spot in red. The real mistake is often at the end of the line just before the red mark, such as a missing ) or :. For crashes that happen while the program runs, right-click a File ... line row of the traceback in the Shell and choose Go to file/line to jump straight there.

#A debugging routine that works

  1. Read the last line of the error. Say the error type out loud; it narrows the cause to a handful of possibilities.
  2. Go to the line number it names. In IDLE, Edit > Go to Line jumps there (Alt+G on Windows and Chromebook, Cmd+J on a Mac). Options > Show Line Numbers puts numbers down the side of your file.
  3. Print your variables right before that line to see what they really hold, not what you think they hold.
  4. Change one thing at a time, and run again after each change.
  5. Still stuck? Explain the code out loud, line by line, to a friend or a rubber duck. You'll often hear yourself say the bug.

⚠️ Watch out

No error doesn't mean no bug. If the program runs but gives the wrong answer, that's a logic error, and Python can't spot those for you. You catch them by testing with inputs where you already know the right answer, like checking that a function says 16 slices fit in 2 pizzas.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1def double(n): return n * 2 is defined. What is double(double(3))?

  • That's double(3). The outer call doubles that answer again.

  • The inner call returns 6, and the outer call doubles 6 to 12. This only works because double returns its answer.

  • double returns a value, so nothing here is None.

  • Passing one function's result into another is completely normal Python.

Show answer

B. The inner call returns 6, and the outer call doubles 6 to 12. This only works because double returns its answer.

2A function show_total(a, b) has just one line in its body: print(a + b). What does result = show_total(2, 3) followed by print(result) display?

  • The function prints 5, but it doesn't return anything, so result doesn't hold 5.

  • The print inside the function shows 5. Then result is None, because a function without return hands back nothing.

  • The function's own print still runs when it's called, so 5 appears first.

Show answer

B. The print inside the function shows 5. Then result is None, because a function without return hands back nothing.

3A traceback has three File lines and ends with TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str. Where should you start reading?

  • The top shows where the chain of calls started, which is the least specific part.

  • The last line says what went wrong, and the line above it says exactly where Python noticed.

  • Each line adds a different piece: what happened, where, and how the program got there.

Show answer

B. The last line says what went wrong, and the line above it says exactly where Python noticed.

4Inside a function you set answer = n * 2. Outside the function, print(answer) crashes. Why?

  • answer is an ordinary variable name.

  • Variables created inside a function vanish when it ends. Return the value and store it in a variable outside.

  • It was; the crash is about where answer can be seen.

Show answer

B. Variables created inside a function vanish when it ends. Return the value and store it in a variable outside.

Key takeaways

  • def name(parameters): defines a function, and nothing in it runs until you call name(...).
  • Define functions above the code that calls them.
  • Arguments fill in parameters by position. Too few gives a TypeError that names the missing one.
  • return hands a value back and ends the function. A function with no return gives back None.
  • Variables made inside a function are local and disappear when it finishes.
  • Read tracebacks bottom up: what happened, then where, then how the program got there.

#Further reading

  • Python Tutorial: Defining Functions (opens in a new tab): the official explanation of def, return, and None.
  • Python Tutorial: Errors and Exceptions (opens in a new tab): the difference between syntax errors and errors that happen while running, with real examples.
  • IDLE documentation (opens in a new tab): every IDLE menu, including Go to Line, Show Line Numbers, and the Debug menu.

What you'll learn

  • Build a program out of small functions that each do one job and return an answer.
  • Test each function on its own with inputs where you already know the right answer.
  • Find and fix a logic error that produces no error message at all.
  • Read a real TypeError, fix it three different ways, and write a helper that keeps asking until the input is valid.

Your club is throwing a pizza party. Ten people are coming, and each will eat 2 slices. How many pizzas do you order? It isn't 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5, because nobody sells half a pizza. It isn't 2 either, because then four people go hungry. The answer is 3, and by the end of this code-along you'll have a planner that gets it right every time, for any party.

Here's how the finished planner fits together. Each box with parentheses is a function that takes something in and hands an answer on to the next step.

Create a new file in IDLE and save it as party.py.

#Step 1: Two tiny functions, and a test

Start with the math. Each function does exactly one job and returns its answer:

// is floor division: it divides and throws away the remainder. The two print lines at the bottom are test calls, and we chose them because we already know the right answers. 16 slices fit exactly in 2 pizzas, and 20 slices need 3.

The first answer is right and the second is wrong. There's no error message, because this is a logic error. Python did exactly what we told it to. We just told it the wrong thing. This is why you test functions with known answers: Python can't warn you about this kind of bug.

#Step 2: Fix the logic bug

20 // 8 is 2, with 4 slices left over. Any leftover slices at all means we need one more pizza. The % operator gives the remainder, so:

Now all four answers are right, including two edge cases: one slice should need 1 pizza, and zero slices should need none. Step through a single call and watch the function's own box on the call stack. pizzas starts at 2, gets bumped to 3, and that's the value handed back.

💡 Tip

Good test inputs come in three kinds: an exact fit (16), a little over (17 or 20), and the smallest possible values (1 and 0). That's where most bugs hide. Testing a five-line function like this takes seconds; hunting the same bug inside a 50-line program can take an hour.

#Step 3: A helper that won't take "ten" for an answer

If someone types ten, int(input(...)) crashes with a ValueError. We'll write a helper function that keeps asking until it gets a whole number. It uses a new string method: text.isdigit() is True only when every character in text is a digit from 0 to 9.

-3 is rejected too, because - isn't a digit. For counting people, that's exactly what we want. Notice that int(text) only runs after the loop, once isdigit() has promised the conversion will work.

The prompt parameter is what makes this helper reusable. The same function can ask "How many guests?" and "Slices per person?" just by being called with different text.

#Step 4: Put the answer in a sentence (and meet a TypeError)

Here's a first attempt at printing the order:

Read it from the bottom up. It's a TypeError, so two types got mixed. The message says + can only join a string to another string, and pizzas is an int. The ^ marks point at the + that failed. Any of these fixes it:

  • Use commas: print("Order", pizzas, "pizzas.")
  • Convert first: print("Order " + str(pizzas) + " pizzas.")
  • Use an f-string: print(f"Order {pizzas} pizzas.")

#Step 5: The finished planner

Everything comes together here. In this run, the user types ten by mistake, then 10 guests, 2 slices each, and $13.50 a pizza:

A few new things appeared:

  • SLICES_PER_PIZZA = 8 is a constant, a value that never changes while the program runs. Writing it in ALL CAPS tells other programmers "don't change this". If your local shop cuts pizzas into 10 slices, you edit one line instead of hunting for every 8.
  • The text in triple quotes under def get_whole_number is a docstring, a short note saying what the function does. It doesn't change how the program runs, but it helps anyone reading your code, including you next month.
  • {cost:.2f} inside an f-string means "show cost with exactly 2 decimal places". Without it, $40.50 would print as $40.5.
  • All the defs come first, then the main program, so every function exists before it's called.

Look at how short the main part is. Each line reads almost like a sentence, because the messy details are tucked away inside well-named functions. That's the real payoff: you can understand the whole program in ten seconds, and dig into any one function only when you need to.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why did we test pizzas_needed with 16, 20, 1, and 0 before building the rest of the program?

  • Python doesn't require tests at all. We added them to catch our own mistakes.

  • That's how the 20 // 8 logic error showed up. It produced no error message, only a wrong number.

  • Test calls actually add a little work. Their value is in catching bugs early.

Show answer

B. That's how the 20 // 8 logic error showed up. It produced no error message, only a wrong number.

2What does the prompt parameter in get_whole_number(prompt) let you do?

  • The same code asks about guests and slices, because the question text is passed in each time.

  • The loop is skipped when isdigit() is True, whatever the prompt says.

  • int(text) makes a whole number. Decimals are handled by float() for the price.

Show answer

A. The same code asks about guests and slices, because the question text is passed in each time.

3Shops near you cut pizzas into 10 slices. What's the smallest change that updates the whole planner?

  • It works if you find them all, but that's exactly the error-prone hunt the constant avoids.

  • Every function uses the constant, so one edit updates the pizza count and the leftovers together.

  • That would give decimal pizzas like 2.5, which is the bug we started with.

Show answer

B. Every function uses the constant, so one edit updates the pizza count and the leftovers together.

Key takeaways

  • Build programs from small functions that each do one job and return the answer.
  • Test each function on its own with inputs whose answers you already know, including edge cases like 0 and 1.
  • A logic error gives no message, only a wrong answer. Tests are how you catch it.
  • A helper like get_whole_number keeps asking until the input is valid, so int() never crashes.
  • TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str is fixed with commas, str(), or an f-string.
  • Constants in ALL CAPS and docstrings make a program easier to change and to read.

#Make it yours

Predict what will happen before you try each of these:

  1. 7 people, 3 slices each, $12 a pizza. That's 21 slices, so you should get 3 pizzas and 3 leftover slices. Does the planner agree?
  2. Type 0 for the number of people. get_whole_number accepts it, but the last line divides by guests. Which error do you get? Change the helper's loop so it also rejects 0.
  3. Type twelve for the price. Write a get_price function that works like get_whole_number but accepts one decimal point. (Hint: text.replace(".", "", 1) removes the first dot, and the result should be all digits.)
  4. Add a second food: drinks, with a price per bottle and one bottle per guest. Write it as a new function and add its cost to the total.

#Further reading

  • Python Tutorial: Defining Functions (opens in a new tab): how def, return, and docstrings work, from the official docs.
  • Python Tutorial: Fancier Output Formatting (opens in a new tab): f-strings and format codes like :.2f, with examples.
  • Python for Everybody: Functions (opens in a new tab): free lecture videos that build functions up from scratch.

What you'll learn

  • Write functions that take parameters and return an answer instead of printing it.
  • Test a function with values whose answers you already know, including the boundaries.
  • Fix syntax, indentation, name, and type errors one at a time by reading each traceback.
  • Find a logic error that produces a wrong answer with no error message.

This set has two halves. Exercises 1 to 4 have you write functions. Exercises 5 and 6 hand you broken code to fix. Debugging is a skill like any other: the more bugs you've met, the faster you recognize the next one, and your capstone will give you plenty of chances.

For every function you write, put a few test calls at the bottom with inputs where you already know the answer. If the function gets those right, you can trust it inside a bigger program.

#Warm-up: follow the calls

Predict all three lines this prints before you step through it. Watch the call stack: a mystery() box appears for each call and disappears when it returns.

The second call is the tricky one. a is 2 by then, so a * 10 is 20, and the function prints got 20 and returns 21. The print inside the function and the value it returns are two separate things.

#Exercise 1: Square it

Write a function square(n) that returns n times n. Then use a for loop to print the squares of 1 through 5.

Need a hint?

The function body is one line, and it starts with return. The printing happens outside the function, in the loop, using whatever square(i) hands back.

Show solution

If you wrote print(n * n) inside the function instead of return, each square would print on its own line, and then the loop's print would show None, because the function handed nothing back.

#Exercise 2: Temperature converter

Write to_fahrenheit(celsius) using the formula F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. Loop over temps_c = [0, 21, 37, 100] and print each conversion.

Need a hint?

Turn the formula straight into a return line. Then loop over the list, calling your function on each item. Which values in the list could you check without a calculator?

Show solution

0 → 32 and 100 → 212 are the freezing and boiling points of water. That makes them perfect test values: you know the answers by heart, so a typo in the formula would jump out immediately.

#Exercise 3: Letter grades

Write letter_grade(score) that returns "A" for 90 and up, "B" for 80 to 89, "C" for 70 to 79, "D" for 60 to 69, and "F" below 60. Test it on [95, 90, 85, 72, 64, 30].

Need a hint?

An if/elif chain with a return in every branch. Start from the top grade and work down; once a branch returns, the function is finished, so later checks don't need an upper limit.

Show solution

Because return ends the function immediately, only one branch can ever answer. Testing exactly 90 checks the boundary, which is where > versus >= mistakes show up.

#Exercise 4: Step counter

Write count_above(numbers, limit) that returns how many items in the list numbers are greater than limit. Use it twice on the same list with two different limits.

Need a hint?

Inside the function, it's the counter pattern from Week 4: start at 0, loop over the list, add 1 when an if is true. The difference is that return count goes at the very end, after the loop.

Show solution

Parameters make the function reusable. The same five lines answer both questions, and they'd work on any list and any limit.

#Exercise 5: Bug hunt

This program should ask for a name and a number, shout the name, and then print the name that many times. It has four bugs. Fix them one at a time: run it, read the error, fix only that one thing, and run again. (.upper() turns text into capital letters.)

Goal output:

Need a hint?

Python reports bugs one at a time, in a fixed order. Problems with how the code is written (colons, indentation) are reported before the program starts. Problems with values (a misspelled name, the wrong type) only appear once the program reaches that line. For the last bug, ask yourself what type input() always gives back.

Show solution

Bug 1. The first run stops before anything happens:

expected ':' on line 1. Add the colon: def shout(word):.

Bug 2. Run again, and Python gets one line further:

The body of repeat isn't indented. Indent print(word * times) so it belongs to the function.

Bug 3. Now the program starts and asks its questions (Sam, then 3), and then:

It's a typo: change nmae to name. For small typos, Python often adds a guess like Did you mean: 'score'? to the end of the message, but nmae is too scrambled for it to suggest anything here.

Bug 4. SAM! prints this time, and then:

input() always hands back a string, so times is "3", not 3, and you can't repeat a string "3" times. Convert it with int(). The fixed program:

Look back at bug 4's traceback. The crash was reported inside repeat on line 5, but the real cause was on line 8, where times was read without int(). A traceback tells you where Python noticed the problem. Sometimes you have to trace backwards to where the bad value came from.

#Exercise 6: The sneaky average

This runs without any error, but average([10, 20, 30]) should be 20.0. Run it, work out why the answer is wrong, and fix it.

Need a hint?

3.33 is 10 divided by 3. So the function divided before it had added up all three numbers. Which line ends a function immediately, and which block is it indented under?

Show solution

The return is indented inside the loop. On the first pass, total is 10, so the function returns 10 / 3 and stops before it ever sees 20 or 30. Move return out one level so it runs after the loop finishes:

When the answer is wrong but there's no error, add print("n:", n, "total:", total) inside the loop. You'd have seen it print only once, which points straight at the bug. In IDLE, Format > Dedent Region moves selected lines one level to the left.

#Challenge: Password checker

Write a program that keeps asking for a password until it's strong enough, and lists every problem each time. A strong password has at least 8 characters, at least one digit, and at least one capital letter. Use at least three functions. ch.isdigit() and ch.isupper() tell you whether a single character is a digit or a capital letter.

Need a hint?

Write has_digit(text) and has_upper(text) first, each returning True or False, and test them on their own. Then write problems(password), which builds and returns a list of messages. An empty list means the password passes, so the main loop can repeat while the list isn't empty.

Show solution

In has_digit, return True sits inside the loop on purpose: as soon as one digit turns up, the answer is known. return False comes after the loop, because you can only say "no digits" once you've checked every character. Compare that with the bug in Exercise 6, where a return inside the loop was exactly the problem.

What you'll learn

  • Know exactly what the capstone program must include and what you hand in.
  • Choose a project idea at a difficulty level you can finish, with room to grow.
  • Plan your inputs, outputs, lists, loops, decisions, and functions before writing code.
  • Write out one run of your program step by step, and use it to find where your loop goes.

For six weeks you've built programs someone else designed. The capstone flips that around. You decide what to build, and you use everything from this course to make it work from start to finish.

In almost every class, the best projects don't come from the most ambitious ideas. They come from students who picked something they genuinely care about, like a quiz on their favorite game, a tool for their sport, or a joke generator for their little brother. Those students keep wanting to make their program better, so they test it more, fix more, and add more.

#The brief

Build a text game, quiz, or tool of your choice in Python that runs in IDLE.

#Your program must use

Requirement Looks like
Variables score = 0, name = input(...)
User input at least one input() the program reacts to
Conditions if / elif / else that make a real decision
A loop for or while, for example a game round or "play again?"
A list storing questions, items, scores, rooms, or answers
At least two functions you define with def, and at least one that takes a parameter or returns a value

#What you hand in

  1. A .py file that runs from top to bottom without crashing on normal use.
  2. A test table showing at least 6 inputs you tried, including unusual ones (a blank answer, letters where a number goes, capital letters, a number that's too big), with what you expected and what actually happened.
  3. One bug you found and fixed, written up in a few sentences: what went wrong, the error message if there was one, and how you fixed it.
  4. A short demo of 2 to 4 minutes, where you run the program and walk through one piece of your code.

The last two lessons in this module walk you through building it in milestones and then testing and presenting it, so you won't face any of this alone.

#The smallest program that ticks every box

If that list looks like a lot, here's a program of about 30 lines that already meets every requirement. Yours will be bigger and much more you, but this proves the list is very doable. In this run, Jordan orders popcorn, lemonade, a menu item that doesn't exist, and more popcorn:

Notice that pick is checked as text ("1") before int() ever sees it. That's why typing 7, or even banana, prints a friendly message instead of crashing. Also notice prices[number - 1]: the menu shows 1, 2, 3, but the list's indexes are 0, 1, 2. That's the same translation you did in the to-do list app.

#Pick a project

Choose one idea, mix two, or invent your own. The levels are a guide to how much work each one takes, not a grade. A polished Starter project beats an unfinished Stretch project every time.

Level Idea What makes it interesting
Starter Dice duel. Two players take turns rolling with random.randint(1, 6); first to 20 wins. A while loop that stops at a target, and a running total for each player
Starter Grade calculator. Enter scores, get the average, the letter grade, and what you need on the final. A list of scores, a letter_grade() function, and input checking
Starter Rock, paper, scissors, best of 5. The computer picks with random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]). if / elif rules for who wins, and a score for each side
Solid Trivia quiz on a topic you know cold: soccer, Minecraft, Marvel, a country, a book series. Questions and answers in two lists, a score, and a percentage at the end
Solid Study flashcards for a real class, which repeat the cards you missed. Moving missed cards into a second list, then looping over that list again
Solid Budget tracker. Add income and expenses, then see the balance and the biggest expense. A menu loop like the to-do app, plus totals and a "biggest so far"
Stretch Word guess (like Hangman). Show _ _ a _, track the letters guessed, and count wrong guesses. Building the display string with a loop over the secret word
Stretch Choose-your-path adventure. Each room is a function, and the player's inventory is a list. Functions that call other functions, and decisions that depend on what's in the list

random.choice(some_list) picks one item from a list at random. It lives in the same random module as randint, so it needs import random at the top of your file too.

💡 Tip

Scope your project so you could finish the basic version in about half the time you have. You can always add features once it works. A small program that runs beats a giant one that crashes, and it gives you something calm to demo.

#Plan before you code

Spend 20 minutes on paper, or in a comment block at the top of your file. It'll save you hours of rewriting later. Copy this template and fill in every line:

Planning in plain words before code has a name: pseudocode. You describe each step the way you'd explain it to a friend, then turn each step into Python later.

#Write out one run, step by step

Next, write down everything a person sees and types during one complete run of your program. This is the script your code has to follow. For a trivia quiz it might be:

Now draw it. Any step that points back to an earlier step is a loop, and every diamond is an if. Here's the quiz script above as a flowchart:

Two backwards arrows means two loops: a for over the questions, inside a while for playing again. You've just designed the structure of your program without writing a line of Python.

#Name your functions now

Good function names are verbs that say what the function does: ask_question, show_menu, roll_dice, get_number, calculate_average. If you can't name a function in two or three words, it's probably doing too many jobs, so split it in two. Look at your flowchart: a box you visit more than once, like "Ask the next question", is a strong candidate for a function.

#Planning mistakes to avoid

⚠️ Watch out

Too big. "An RPG with 20 levels, shops, and a boss fight" won't fit. "One dungeon with 3 rooms and a key" will, and it can still be great.

No list. If your idea doesn't naturally need one, find a place it helps: past guesses, high scores, menu items, questions.

Functions as an afterthought. Plan at least two now. Squeezing them in at the end means rewriting code that already works.

Key takeaways

  • The capstone needs variables, input, conditions, a loop, a list, and at least two of your own functions.
  • You hand in four things: the .py file, a test table, one bug write-up, and a short demo.
  • Pick a project you care about, at a size you can finish in half your time.
  • Plan on paper first: inputs, outputs, lists, loops, decisions, and function names.
  • Write out one full run. Backwards arrows become loops, and repeated steps become functions.

#Further reading

  • Python docs: the random module (opens in a new tab): randint, choice, and shuffle for games with dice, cards, or random picks.
  • The Big Book of Small Python Projects (opens in a new tab): free online, packed with short text games to borrow ideas from.

What you'll learn

  • Start your capstone from a skeleton file that already runs.
  • Build in five milestones, so the program works at the end of every one.
  • Clean up answers with .strip() and .lower() so capital letters and stray spaces don't matter.
  • Follow a complete quiz from first draft to finished program, and see how its functions call each other.

The fastest way to get stuck on a project is to type 100 lines and press F5 for the first time. You'll get an error on line 12, fix it, get another on line 40, and never know how many are left. Instead, build in milestones. Each milestone ends with a version of your program that runs. If milestone 3 breaks, the bug is in what you added since milestone 2, not anywhere in 100 lines.

💡 Tip

Before you start each milestone, use File > Save As... to save a copy with the milestone in its name: project_m2.py, project_m3.py, and so on. If something goes badly wrong, you can open the last version that worked and carry on from there.

#The starter skeleton

Copy this into a new file. It already runs, and it has a home for every capstone requirement. In this test run the user answers y, then maybe (which isn't allowed), then N with spaces around a capital N:

get_choice uses two string tools you'll want in almost every project:

  • .strip() removes spaces from the start and end, so " N " becomes "N".
  • .lower() makes everything lowercase, so "N" becomes "n".

Chained together, input(prompt).strip().lower() means the user can type Y, y, or y and your program understands all three. Then choice not in options is True whenever the answer isn't one of the allowed ones, which keeps the loop asking.

#The five milestones

Milestone Goal Done when...
M1: Skeleton Fill in the header comments, the welcome message, and the main loop it runs, and "Go again?" works
M2: Core, once Your data in a list and the main feature working one time, even if the code is messy one full round works with normal input
M3: Functions Move the core into functions that take parameters and return values the main program is short and readable
M4: Results and repeat Score, totals, or a summary, plus play again or a menu a whole session works from start to finish
M5: Polish Input checking, friendly messages, and extra features it survives your test table (next lesson)

Now watch one project go through all five.

#Worked example: Space Trivia

The plan: a five-question space quiz. Questions and answers live in two lists. At the end it shows the score as a percentage with a message, lets you play again, and remembers your best score.

#M1: Skeleton

M1 is the skeleton above with the header comments filled in and the welcome changed to === Space Trivia ===. It's boring, and that's fine. It runs, and the play-again loop already works.

#M2: The core, once, with no functions yet

Get the main idea working in the simplest way you can. Here that means two parallel lists, where questions[0] goes with answers[0], questions[1] with answers[1], and so on. In this run the player gets two right and one wrong:

It works, as long as you type carefully. (A bug is hiding in here, and the test table in the next lesson will catch it.) A list can be split across several lines like questions is, as long as the brackets match, which makes long items much easier to read.

#M3: Move the repeated work into functions

What does the program do over and over? It asks one question and checks the answer. That's the first function. It returns True or False, and the code that called it decides what to do about the score.

The second function runs the whole quiz once and returns the score:

if ask_question(...) works because the function hands back a Boolean, just like if is_even(n) in the Week 6 notes.

#M4: Results and play again

show_result turns the score into a percentage and picks a message. get_yes_no is the skeleton's get_choice made specific to y/n answers. The main loop calls them, and it remembers the best score with the same "keep the biggest so far" pattern you used on the receipt exercise in Week 5.

#M5: Polish

The last pass added two more questions, a welcome that explains the rules, and a goodbye that shows the best score. The .strip().lower() cleanup inside ask_question from M3 means capital letters and stray spaces no longer matter.

Here's how the finished program's functions call one another during one round. The main program only talks to run_quiz and show_result; run_quiz does the asking by calling ask_question once per question.

#The finished program

In this sample session the player types mercury in lowercase, gets the largest planet wrong, adds stray spaces before milky way, shouts MARS, types yes at the play-again question (which isn't accepted), and then quits with n:

Typing y instead would start a fresh round with the score back at 0, because run_quiz sets score = 0 every time it's called. Meanwhile best lives in the main program, outside the loop, so it remembers the highest score across rounds.

#Requirements check

  • Variables: score, best, playing, reply
  • Input: every answer, plus the play-again question
  • Conditions: right or wrong, the percentage message, and the y/n check
  • Loops: for over the questions, and while for replaying and for checking input
  • Lists: questions and answers
  • Functions: five, including ask_question, which takes parameters and returns a value

#When you get stuck

  • Run after every few lines. Small steps mean small bugs.
  • Read the traceback from the bottom up, then jump to the line it names (Edit > Go to Line in IDLE).
  • Print your variables where things go wrong, and delete those prints once it's fixed.
  • Go back a milestone. If the current version is a mess, open your last saved copy and redo just the newest piece.
  • Ask with specifics. "On line 23 I get IndexError, and i is 5 when it crashes" gets you an answer much faster than "it doesn't work".

Key takeaways

  • Start from a skeleton that runs, and keep it running at the end of every milestone.
  • Save a copy before each milestone so you can always go back to a working version.
  • Get the core working once in the simplest way, then move repeated work into functions.
  • .strip().lower() on every answer makes your program forgiving about spaces and capitals.
  • Parallel lists keep matching data together: questions[i] goes with answers[i].

#Further reading

  • Python docs: string methods (opens in a new tab): strip(), lower(), isdigit(), and many more you can use in your capstone.
  • Python Tutorial: Defining Functions (opens in a new tab): a refresher on parameters and return values.
